teile.einleitung: A bike helmet protects your head if you fall. For it to really help, it has to fit properly and be fastened. A helmet also makes sense on a scooter or a skateboard.
wichtigste: The helmet sits straight, just above the eyebrows at the front.
There is room for one or two fingers between the chin strap and the chin.
A helmet only protects you if it is fastened.
Inside, the helmet is usually made of hard foam, which absorbs the impact.
After a bad fall you replace the helmet.
A helmet also makes sense on a scooter, a skateboard and inline skates.

abschnitte.text: Inside, the bike helmet has a thick layer of **hard foam**. On impact this foam squashes together and **absorbs the blow**. So less force reaches your head. On the outside a thin plastic shell protects it. Air vents make sure it does not get too hot under the helmet.

A good helmet sits **straight** on your head and covers your forehead. At the front it should be **just above your eyebrows**. It must not slide backwards and leave your forehead uncovered. With a little dial at the back of your head you can make it tighter or looser. When you shake your head, the helmet should not wobble.

The helmet must **always be fastened** when you ride. An open helmet can fall off your head in a fall. The **chin strap** should fit snugly but not press. About **one or two fingers** should fit between the strap and your chin. The side straps meet just below your ears.

After a **bad fall** you need a new helmet. The foam may be damaged inside even if you cannot see anything from outside. Old helmets should also be replaced after a few years. You can also fall on a **scooter**, a **skateboard** or **inline skates**. That is why a helmet makes sense there too, and when skiing as well.

gewusst: On fast e-bikes with motor assistance up to 45 km/h, a helmet is compulsory in Switzerland.
You should not wear a bike helmet when climbing on playgrounds, because the straps can get caught.

teile.einleitung: Lightning is a giant electrical discharge that happens during thunderstorms between clouds or between a cloud and the ground. At up to about 30,000 degrees Celsius it is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The loud thunder we hear afterwards is caused by this enormous heat.
wichtigste: Lightning is an electrical discharge in the air.
It gets as hot as about 30,000 degrees, hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Lightning forms in large thunderclouds.
Thunder happens because the air expands suddenly.
You can estimate how far away a storm is with the rule of thumb: seconds divided by three.
A lightning conductor protects buildings from lightning damage.
You are well protected in a car during a thunderstorm.

abschnitte.text: In a tall **thundercloud**, tiny ice grains and water droplets rub against each other. This separates electrical charges: positive ones gather at the top, negative ones at the bottom. If the voltage gets too great, it evens itself out with a flash of lightning. A flash usually lasts only a fraction of a second; it often flickers because several **discharges** follow one after another.

In the lightning channel the air heats up to about **30,000 degrees Celsius**. The surface of the Sun, by contrast, is only about 5500 degrees. But the lightning channel is only a few centimetres thick. The heat makes the air expand explosively, and that creates **thunder**.

abschnitte.titel: How far away is the storm?
abschnitte.text: Light reaches us almost instantly, but sound takes about three seconds to travel one kilometre. If you count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder and divide by three, you get roughly the distance in kilometres. So at 9 seconds the storm is about 3 kilometres away. If the gap is less than 30 seconds, you should look for **shelter**.

The **lightning conductor** was invented around 1750 by the American Benjamin Franklin. It carries the current safely into the ground through a wire. In a car or a house you are well protected, because the metal shell acts like a **Faraday cage**. Outdoors you should not stand under single trees or swim in a lake, and if there is danger you should crouch down with your feet together.

Worldwide, about 40 to 50 flashes of lightning strike every second. In Switzerland there is the most lightning in **Ticino**, because there warm, damp air meets the Alps in summer. The transmitter tower on the **Säntis** is struck very often every year and is therefore used for lightning research. Lightning also causes forest fires and power cuts.

begriffe.erklaerung: When built-up electrical charge suddenly evens itself out.
A very tall cloud in which lightning forms, also called cumulonimbus.
A metal rod with a wire that carries lightning safely into the ground.
A metal shell that protects the inside from electric current.

gewusst: Lightning can certainly strike the same place twice; tall towers are in fact hit often.
If lightning strikes sand, it can melt it into glass tubes called fulgurites.

teile.einleitung: Your pulse shows how many times your heart beats in a minute. You can feel it at certain places on your body. In sport your pulse helps you judge how hard you are working and how good your endurance is.
wichtigste: You can feel your pulse easily on your wrist or your neck.
The resting pulse of adults is about 60 to 80 beats per minute.
In children the resting pulse is a little higher.
The beats in 15 seconds times four gives your pulse per minute.
A trained heart beats more slowly at rest.
A pulse that falls quickly after exercise shows good endurance.

abschnitte.text: With every heartbeat blood is pumped into the **arteries**. You can feel this pressure wave as your **pulse**. On the **wrist**, on the thumb side, an artery lies close under the skin. You put two fingers there, not your thumb, because your thumb has a pulse of its own. Your pulse is also easy to feel on your **neck** next to your larynx.

You do not have to count for a whole minute. If you count for **15 seconds**, you multiply **by 4**: 18 beats give 72 per minute. If you count for **10 seconds**, you multiply **by 6**: 25 beats give 150 per minute. After sport it is better to count for a short time, because your pulse falls quickly. Many sports watches also measure your pulse automatically.

At rest an adult's heart usually beats about **60 to 80 times** a minute. In **children** the resting pulse is a little higher. Athletes with good endurance training often have a low resting pulse. Their heart has a larger **stroke volume** and pumps more blood with each beat. So it needs fewer beats for the same amount of blood.

When you exert yourself, your pulse rises because your muscles need more oxygen. After the effort it falls again. The **recovery pulse** shows how quickly this happens. In well-trained people the pulse falls faster. That is why it is a sign of good **endurance**.

gewusst: In newborn babies the heart often beats well over 100 times a minute at rest.
A well-known rule of thumb for the highest pulse is: 220 minus your age. But it is only a rough guide.

teile.einleitung: **Sonata form** is one of the most important forms in classical music. Many first movements of sonatas, symphonies and string quartets are built this way. It works a little like a story: themes are introduced, transformed and come back at the end.
wichtigste: The three main sections are called exposition, development and recapitulation.
In the exposition two themes are introduced.
In a movement in a major key the second theme is usually in the dominant.
In classical works the exposition is often repeated.
After the recapitulation a coda can round off the movement.

abschnitte.text: In the **exposition** the composer introduces the themes. First the **first subject** is heard in the home key. After a transition comes the **second subject**, which is often calmer and more song-like. In a movement in a major key it is usually in the **dominant**, so with C major it is in G major. In minor keys the music usually moves to the relative major. In classical works **repeat signs** show that the exposition is played twice.

In the **development** the themes are worked on. The composer breaks them up into small motifs, lets them travel through different keys and combines them in new ways. This is often where the greatest tension of the movement arises. At the end of the development the music leads back to the home key and prepares for the return.

In the **recapitulation** the themes of the exposition come back. This time the second subject is also in the **home key**. In this way the tension between the keys is resolved. After that a **coda** may follow, Italian for tail. It rounds off the movement and can be very long in Beethoven's music.

Sonata form got its classical shape with **Haydn**, **Mozart** and **Beethoven**. Some movements also begin with a slow **introduction**. Later Romantic composers changed the form more and more freely. The name “sonata form” only comes from music theorists of the 19th century, who described what composers had long been doing.

gewusst: The name does not mean a whole sonata, but the form of a single movement in it.
Many film scores and overtures also use the idea of introduction, working-out and return.

teile.einleitung: International sports organisations are federations that organise sport around the world, set the rules and hold big competitions such as the Olympic Games or world championships. An astonishing number of them have their headquarters in Switzerland. That is why Lausanne is even called the “Olympic Capital”.
wichtigste: The International Olympic Committee IOC was founded in Paris in 1894 and today has its headquarters in Lausanne.
Since June 2025 Kirsty Coventry has been at the head of the IOC.
The world football federation FIFA was founded in 1904 and is based in Zurich.
The Union of European Football Associations UEFA has its headquarters in Nyon.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport CAS in Lausanne decides disputes in sport.
Since 2019 the world athletics federation has been called World Athletics.
The ski and snowboard federation FIS is based in Oberhofen on Lake Thun, the cycling federation UCI in Aigle.

abschnitte.text: The **International Olympic Committee** was founded in Paris in 1894 on the initiative of Pierre de Coubertin. Since 1915 its headquarters have been in **Lausanne**. The IOC awards the Olympic Games to host cities and watches over the Olympic rules. Since June 2025 **Kirsty Coventry** from Zimbabwe has been president; she is the first woman in this office. The Olympic Museum is also in Lausanne.

**FIFA** was founded in Paris in 1904 and today has its headquarters in **Zurich**. It organises the women's and men's football World Cups. Its president since 2016 has been Gianni Infantino, who was born in Brig in Valais. **UEFA** is the European football federation; it was founded in Basel in 1954 and is now based in Nyon on Lake Geneva. It organises the European Championship and the Champions League.

abschnitte.titel: The Court of Arbitration for Sport
abschnitte.text: The **Court of Arbitration for Sport**, abbreviated CAS, was founded in 1984 and has its seat in Lausanne. It is an arbitration court that decides disputes in sport. These are often about doping cases, bans or the question of who may take part in a competition. At big events such as the Olympic Games the CAS even sets up its own courts on site.

Almost every sport has its own **world federation**. Since 2019 the world athletics federation has been called **World Athletics**, and it is based in Monaco. The International Ski and Snowboard Federation FIS has its headquarters in **Oberhofen** on Lake Thun, and the cycling federation UCI in **Aigle** in the canton of Vaud. The basketball federation FIBA is based in Mies, whereas the International Paralympic Committee IPC is in Bonn in Germany. The World Anti-Doping Agency WADA has its headquarters in Montreal in Canada.

About 50 international sports organisations have their headquarters in Switzerland. Reasons for this are political **neutrality**, the central location in Europe and how easy it is to get there. Many federations are organised as associations under Swiss law, which is simple and flexible. The organisations bring jobs and international visitors, but they are also sometimes criticised because of scandals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A union of clubs or countries with shared aims.
The International Olympic Committee, which awards and oversees the Olympic Games.
A court that decides disputes outside the ordinary courts.
A country's policy of not taking sides in conflicts.
The person who leads an organisation and represents it to the outside world.

gewusst: In 2019 the IOC opened its headquarters, Olympic House, in Vidy near Lausanne.
UEFA was founded in Basel in 1954 but only later moved to Lake Geneva.
Both FIFA president Gianni Infantino and his predecessor Sepp Blatter come from Upper Valais.

teile.einleitung: Apollo 11 was the first space mission in which people landed on the Moon. On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin touched down on the Moon’s surface in the lunar module Eagle. Hundreds of millions of people watched the event live on television.
wichtigste: Apollo 11 was a mission of the American space agency NASA.
The Saturn V rocket launched on 16 July 1969 in Florida.
Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
In 1969 Buzz Aldrin became the second person to walk on the Moon.
Michael Collins stayed in the spacecraft Columbia in orbit around the Moon.
The astronauts brought about 22 kilograms of moon rock back to Earth.
An experiment from the University of Bern went to the Moon too.

abschnitte.text: In the 1960s the USA and the Soviet Union competed in the **space race**. In 1961 President John F. Kennedy had promised to put people on the Moon before the end of the decade. On 16 July 1969 Apollo 11 lifted off with the huge **Saturn V** rocket from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The rocket was over 100 metres tall, taller than a church tower. Three days later the astronauts reached orbit around the Moon.

There were three astronauts on board. **Neil Armstrong** was the commander. **Buzz Aldrin** flew the lunar module Eagle down to the surface with him. Michael Collins stayed in the command module **Columbia** and circled the Moon alone. He had to pick the other two up again later.

On 20 July 1969 the Eagle landed in the **Sea of Tranquillity**, a flat, dark plain on the Moon. Because there were large boulders at the planned landing site, Armstrong steered the module by hand at the end, until only a little fuel was left. A few hours later Armstrong climbed down the ladder and became the first person to set foot on the Moon. In Switzerland it was early in the morning of 21 July. About 20 minutes later Buzz Aldrin followed as the second person.

Armstrong and Aldrin stayed outside on the Moon for about two and a half hours. They collected rock samples, took photos and set up measuring instruments. One of these was the **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern, led by Johannes Geiss. It was a sheet of aluminium foil that caught particles from the Sun, and it was even set up before the American flag. The foil was brought back to Earth and examined in Bern.

On 24 July 1969 the capsule landed safely in the **Pacific Ocean**. Afterwards the astronauts had to spend three weeks in quarantine, because people feared they might bring back moon germs. Five more Apollo missions landed by 1972; altogether twelve people walked on the Moon. Nobody has been there since. With the **Artemis** programme, NASA wants to send people to the Moon again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space agency of the USA.
A small spacecraft that lands on the Moon and takes off again.
The huge rocket that carried the Apollo spacecraft into space.
A stream of tiny particles that flows out from the Sun.
A time when you are kept apart from others for safety.

gewusst: Armstrong’s and Aldrin’s footprints can probably still be seen on the Moon today, because there is no wind there.
The Bern solar wind sail was the only non-American experiment on Apollo 11.
Buzz Aldrin’s real name was Edwin Aldrin; he later officially changed his first name to Buzz.

teile.einleitung: Big Ben is one of the best-known landmarks of London. Many people think the name refers to the clock tower at Parliament, but it actually means the largest bell in the tower. The tower itself has officially been called the Elizabeth Tower since 2012.
wichtigste: Strictly speaking, Big Ben is the name of the largest bell in the tower.
Since 2012 the tower has been called the Elizabeth Tower.
It is part of the Palace of Westminster, the seat of the British Parliament.
The bell weighs about 13.7 tonnes.
The clock has been running since 1859.
The tower is about 96 metres tall.
From 2017 to 2022 the tower underwent major renovation.

abschnitte.text: The great bell **Big Ben** was cast in London in 1858 and weighs about 13.7 tonnes. It strikes every hour on the hour. A first bell cracked during tests and had to be recast. The second bell also soon developed a **crack**, so it was turned slightly and a lighter hammer is used.

The tower stands at the northern end of the **Palace of Westminster** on the Thames. It is about 96 metres tall and was designed by the architect Augustus Pugin. On all four sides there is a large **clock face** about 7 metres across. In 2012 it was renamed **Elizabeth Tower** for Queen Elizabeth II’s Diamond Jubilee, her 60 years on the throne.

The old Palace of Westminster burnt down almost completely in 1834. When it was rebuilt, a particularly accurate clock was to be made as well. It has shown the time since 1859 and is considered very reliable. Nobody is quite sure where the name Big Ben comes from; often **Sir Benjamin Hall**, who was in charge of the building work at the time, is mentioned.

From 2017 to 2022 the tower was thoroughly **renovated**. During this time Big Ben was mostly silent and rang only on special occasions such as New Year’s Eve. The clock is still wound and checked by hand today. To adjust the clock finely, old **penny coins** are placed on the pendulum.

Big Ben can be seen on countless postcards and in many films. The chimes are broadcast by the BBC on the radio, for example on New Year’s Eve. Together with the Palace of Westminster, the tower has been a **UNESCO World Heritage** site since 1987. Anyone who climbs the tower on a guided tour has to climb over 300 steps to reach the bell.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal body that rings loudly when struck.
The surface of a clock with the numbers and hands.
The assembly of a country’s elected representatives.
A swinging weight that makes a clock run regularly.

gewusst: A single penny coin on the pendulum makes the clock gain about two fifths of a second per day.
Big Ben rings the note E.

teile.einleitung: Film theory deals with the question of how films work and why they affect us. It examines pictures, editing, sound and storytelling and asks what a film says about the world and society. Many of its terms help us understand films more precisely.
wichtigste: Film theory examines how films are made and how they affect viewers.
The Kuleshov effect shows that a picture is interpreted differently depending on the picture before it.
The diegesis is the story world of the plot.
Film music that only the audience hears is called non-diegetic sound.
Sergei Eisenstein developed the theory of the “montage of attractions”.
André Bazin defended long takes and depth of field as a realistic alternative to montage.
In 1975 Laura Mulvey coined the term “male gaze”.

abschnitte.text: **Film theory** is part of film studies, which you can study at universities. It asks what is special about film as an art form. It also examines how pictures, editing and sound trigger feelings and thoughts in viewers. Some theories see films as a mirror of **society**. If you know film theory, you notice how much planning goes into every shot.

Around 1920 the Russian filmmaker **Lev Kuleshov** carried out an experiment. He cut the same neutral face of an actor once next to a plate of soup and once next to a child in a coffin. The viewers believed they saw hunger or grief in the face, even though it was always the same. This **Kuleshov effect** shows that meaning only arises through the connection of pictures. Connecting shots is called **montage**.

The Soviet director **Sergei Eisenstein** developed the theory of the “montage of attractions”. He wanted pictures to collide so hard that they shook the audience up, for example in “Battleship Potemkin” from 1925. The French film critic **André Bazin** saw things differently. He defended long shots without cuts, the **long take**, and great depth of field. In this way, he said, viewers could discover for themselves what was important, and the film would seem more realistic.

The **diegesis** is the story world of the plot, that is everything the characters themselves experience. Music from a radio in the film is diegetic, because the characters hear it. Film music that only the audience hears is called **non-diegetic sound**. The **mise en scène** includes everything visible in the picture, such as the set, lighting, costumes and the actors' performance. When a character speaks straight into the camera, it is called breaking the fourth wall.

abschnitte.titel: Auteur cinema and the Nouvelle Vague
abschnitte.text: In the 1950s young critics wrote for the French film magazine **Cahiers du cinéma**. They developed the “politique des auteurs”, the idea that the director is the real author of a film, like a writer of a book. Some of them, such as François Truffaut and the Paris-born Swiss Jean-Luc Godard, soon made films themselves. This movement was called the **Nouvelle Vague**, the new wave. It changed cinema with freer ways of telling stories and filming in the street.

In 1975 the British film theorist **Laura Mulvey** coined the term **male gaze**. By this she meant that in many films women are shown mainly as men see them. Other theories examine how films portray different cultures, groups or history. The German sociologist Siegfried Kracauer, for example, asked what films reveal about the mood of a period. In this way film theory helps us watch films critically and consciously.

begriffe.erklaerung: Putting individual shots together into a scene.
The story world of a film in which the characters live.
A long scene filmed without a cut in a single shot.
Everything that can be seen in the picture, such as the set, lighting and acting.
The invisible boundary between the film and the audience.

gewusst: The Odessa Steps scene from “Battleship Potemkin” is still imitated in films today.
The term fourth wall comes from the theatre, where the stage has three real walls and one open side facing the audience.
Jean-Luc Godard lived for many years in Rolle on Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Folk dances are traditional dances of a region or a people that have been handed down. They are often danced at festivals, frequently in traditional costume. Every country has its own dances with typical music and typical steps.
wichtigste: The Ländler is an old turning dance in triple time from the Alpine region.
Many folk dance groups in Switzerland wear traditional costume when they perform.
The polka comes from Bohemia, which today belongs to the Czech Republic.
In the Schuhplattler from Bavaria and Tyrol the dancers slap their shoes and thighs.
Flamenco comes from Spain, sirtaki from Greece, tarantella from Italy and csárdás from Hungary.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland many **folk dance groups** and costume societies keep old dances alive. When they perform they often wear a **traditional costume**, that is the traditional clothing of their region. Every canton and some valleys have their own costumes. They dance to **Ländler music** with the Schwyzerörgeli, clarinet and double bass. You can see the groups at village festivals, on 1 August or at costume festivals.

The **Ländler** is a couple dance from the Alpine region in **triple time**. The partners turn together in a circle. Later the **waltz** developed from the Ländler. The **polka** began in the 19th century in **Bohemia** and is a lively couple dance in duple time. It quickly became popular all over Europe, including Switzerland.

The **Schuhplattler** is a folk dance from **Bavaria** and **Tyrol**. The men jump and slap the soles of their shoes, their knees and their thighs with their hands in time to the music. The slapping noise is part of the music. The women often spin around on the spot at the same time. The dance requires a lot of practice and good fitness.

**Flamenco** comes from Andalusia in the south of **Spain**; guitar, clapping and stamping are typical. The **sirtaki** from **Greece** is danced in a line, with arms on the neighbours' shoulders. The **tarantella** is a fast dance from southern Italy. The **csárdás** from **Hungary** often begins slowly and then becomes very fast.

gewusst: The sirtaki only became world-famous through the film “Zorba the Greek” from 1964.
The name Ländler comes from the “Landl”, an area in Upper Austria.

teile.einleitung: Cycling includes all the sports in which you race on a bike. They include road races such as the Tour de France, races on the track, mountain biking and BMX. Switzerland has a long cycling tradition and many successful riders.
wichtigste: The most famous cycle race is the Tour de France.
The leader of the Tour de France wears a yellow jersey.
In a time trial each rider rides alone against the clock.
The big cycle race through Switzerland is called the Tour de Suisse.
Nino Schurter became Olympic mountain bike champion in 2016.
So that a bike can be seen well in the dark, it needs a light.
You stop the bike with the brake.

abschnitte.text: In **road cycling** the professionals ride one-day races or stage races lasting many days. On the **track**, riders race in a velodrome with steep bends. **Mountain biking** goes through forests and over stones, and BMX over jumps and bends. Other forms are cyclo-cross across country and artistic cycling indoors.

The **Tour de France** has taken place every year in July since 1903 and lasts three weeks. The riders cover over 3000 kilometres, including high passes in the Alps and the Pyrenees. The leader of the overall classification wears the **yellow jersey**. There is also a green jersey for the best sprinter and a white one with red polka dots for the best climber. Together with the Giro d'Italia and the Vuelta in Spain, it is one of the three Grand Tours.

In a **time trial** each rider starts alone and rides against the clock; whoever needs the shortest time wins. In normal races the professionals ride in teams and help each other. In the slipstream of the rider in front you need much less effort, which is why the field often rides close together. This field is also called the peloton.

The **Tour de Suisse** has been held since 1933 and goes over many Swiss passes. Ferdi Kübler and Hugo Koblet won the Tour de France in 1950 and 1951. **Fabian Cancellara** became Olympic time trial champion in 2008 and 2016. **Nino Schurter** from the Grisons won Olympic gold in mountain biking in Rio in 2016 and became world champion many times. The world cycling federation UCI has its headquarters in Aigle in the canton of Vaud.

In everyday life the **bike** is a popular way of getting to school. In the dark it needs a white **light** at the front and a red one at the back so that you can be seen clearly. Working **brakes** are compulsory so that you can stop in time. A bike helmet protects your head if you fall. In many Swiss schools children learn the traffic rules in the cycling test.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large main group of riders in a cycle race.
The area behind a rider where there is less air resistance.
A race in which each rider rides alone against the clock.
The jersey of the leader of the overall classification in the Tour de France.
A cycle race over several days with many stages.

gewusst: The yellow jersey is yellow because the newspaper that founded the Tour was printed on yellow paper.
Tour de France riders often burn over 6000 kilocalories on a hard mountain stage.
Ferdi Kübler lived to be 97 and was for a long time the oldest living Tour winner.

teile.einleitung: Basketball is a fast ball game in which two teams try to throw the ball into the opponents' basket. It was invented in the USA in 1891 and is now one of the most popular sports in the world. It is mostly played indoors, but also outside on courts.
wichtigste: Each team has five players on the court at the same time.
You score points by throwing the ball into the basket.
If you move with the ball, you have to dribble it, that is bounce it on the floor.
A basket from behind the three-point line counts 3 points, a free throw 1 point.
The basket hangs about 3 metres high.
Basketball was invented in the USA.
In the very first game a peach basket was used as the basket.

abschnitte.text: Two teams of **five** players each are on the court. The aim is to throw the ball through the opponents' **basket** and to score more points than the other team. With the ball in your hand you may not simply walk; you have to **dribble** it. Team-mates pass the ball to each other to find a good shooting position. The defenders try to stop shots and win the ball.

A normal basket during play counts **2 points**. If you shoot from behind the three-point line, you get **3 points**. A successful **free throw** after a foul counts 1 point. Because so many baskets are scored, games often end with 80 or even more than 100 points per team.

The game was invented by the PE teacher **James Naismith** in the winter of 1891 in Springfield in the US state of Massachusetts. He was looking for a game his students could play indoors. As baskets he hung two **peach baskets** from a balcony, about 3 metres high. After every basket someone had to fetch the ball out with a ladder; only later was the bottom cut out of the basket.

The most famous league in the world is the **NBA** in North America, with stars such as Michael Jordan and LeBron James. Basketball has been an Olympic sport since 1936. The world federation FIBA has its headquarters in Mies in the canton of Vaud. **Clint Capela** from Geneva is one of the best-known Swiss basketball players and plays in the NBA. In Switzerland basketball is particularly popular in French-speaking Switzerland and in Ticino.

You need a ball, two baskets and good indoor shoes. The basket consists of a metal ring with a net, attached to a board. Under international rules the court is 28 metres long and 15 metres wide. Outdoors people often also play **3x3**, a fast version with three players per team on one basket, which has been an Olympic sport since 2021.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bouncing the ball on the floor again and again with one hand while moving.
An undisturbed shot from the free-throw line after a foul.
A curved line around the basket; a basket from behind it gives 3 points.
The most famous professional basketball league, in North America.
When a player pushes the ball straight down into the basket from above.

gewusst: James Naismith, the inventor of basketball, came from Canada.
The first basketball rules had only 13 points.
The world federation FIBA has its headquarters in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Sports nutrition is about what athletes should eat and drink in order to train well and recover quickly. For exercise the body needs energy from carbohydrates, fat and protein. If you eat the right foods at the right time, you can perform better.
wichtigste: One gram of fat supplies about 9 kilocalories, one gram of carbohydrate or protein about 4.
Carbohydrates are stored in the muscle as glycogen.
With carb-loading you fill the glycogen stores to the maximum before a marathon.
Strength athletes are recommended about 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.
An isotonic drink has the same osmotic pressure as the blood.
Too much plain water during long competitions can lead to hyponatraemia.
Vitamin C improves the absorption of iron from plants.

abschnitte.text: Energy is measured in **kilocalories** (kcal). One gram of carbohydrate or protein supplies about 4 kcal, one gram of fat about 9 kcal. A bar with 40 grams of carbohydrate, 10 grams of fat and 5 grams of protein therefore supplies about 270 kcal. The body stores carbohydrates as **glycogen** in the muscles and the liver. These stores are the most important source of energy during intense sport.

Bread, pasta, rice, potatoes and fruit are rich in carbohydrates. With **carb-loading**, endurance athletes eat especially large amounts of carbohydrates in the days before a marathon to fill their glycogen stores to the maximum. The **glycaemic index** shows how quickly a food makes blood sugar rise. Glucose, that is grape sugar, is usually used as the reference value of 100.

The body needs protein to build and repair muscles. Expert societies recommend that strength athletes eat about 1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Good sources are dairy products, eggs, meat, fish, pulses and tofu. The permitted dietary supplement **creatine** increases the phosphocreatine stores in the muscle and helps with short, hard efforts.

During sport you lose water and salts through sweat. **Isotonic** drinks have the same osmotic pressure as the blood and are absorbed quickly. Anyone who drinks only large amounts of plain water during very long competitions risks **hyponatraemia**, that is too little sodium in the blood. This can become dangerous, which is why a little salt belongs in the drink.

Iron is important for carrying oxygen in the blood. Vitamin C, for example from oranges or peppers, improves the absorption of **iron** from plants. Since 2004 caffeine has no longer been on the Prohibited List of the World Anti-Doping Agency WADA. For children and teenagers a varied diet following the food pyramid is usually better than powders and pills.

begriffe.erklaerung: The storage form of carbohydrates in the muscles and liver.
Deliberately filling up the carbohydrate stores before a competition.
Having the same particle pressure as the blood, and therefore quickly absorbed.
Too little salt (sodium) in the blood.
A substance made by the body that supplies the muscles with quick energy.

gewusst: One gram of fat supplies more than twice as much energy as one gram of sugar.
A marathon runner often uses about 2500 to 3000 kilocalories in a race.
During hard endurance exercise the glycogen stores last only about 90 minutes.

teile.einleitung: A scale is a series of notes that rises or falls step by step, like the steps of a staircase. It provides the notes from which melodies and chords are built. The best-known scales are major and minor, but there are many others in the world.
wichtigste: A major scale consists of seven different notes; the eighth is the octave.
The C major scale needs no sharps or flats at all.
In major the semitone steps are between the 3rd and 4th and between the 7th and 8th degrees.
The relative key of C major is A minor.
An octave spans twelve semitones.
A pentatonic scale has five different notes.
G major has one sharp in its key signature.

abschnitte.text: Scales are made of **whole-tone steps** and **semitone steps**. On the piano a semitone is the distance to the key directly next to it, for example from E to F. A whole tone is made of two semitones, as from C to D. A whole octave spans twelve semitones. If you play all twelve one after the other, you get the **chromatic scale**.

A **major scale** has seven different notes, and the eighth note is the octave. The semitone steps are between the 3rd and 4th and between the 7th and 8th degrees; all the other steps are whole tones. The C major scale C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C needs no sharps or flats and uses only white keys. Other major scales need sharps or flats; for example, G major has one sharp, namely F sharp.

To many people minor sounds rather sad or serious, while major sounds cheerful and bright. In the natural **minor scale** the semitone steps are between the 2nd and 3rd and between the 5th and 6th degrees. Every major key has a **relative minor** with the same key signature; A minor belongs to C major. There are also the harmonic and melodic minor scales with slightly changed degrees.

The **pentatonic scale** has only five different notes and no semitone steps. It is found in folk songs all over the world, for example in China, Africa, Scotland and in the blues. On the piano the five black keys make a pentatonic scale. In Arabic and Indian music there are scales with notes that lie between our semitones.

Many music students practise scales to make their fingers nimble and to get to know the keys. When singing, people often use the syllables do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti; this is called **solmisation**. For the order of the sharp keys G, D, A, E, B and F sharp there is a German memory sentence, “Geh Du Alter Esel, Hole Fisch” (“Go, you old donkey, fetch fish”), in which the H stands for B. The circle of fifths shows all the keys with their key signatures at a glance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest distance between two notes in our music.
The distance from the first to the eighth note of a scale.
A scale made of five different notes.
A major and a minor key with the same key signature.
A scale made of all twelve semitones of the octave.

gewusst: On the black keys of the piano you can almost never improvise wrongly, because they form a pentatonic scale.
In the song “Do-Re-Mi” from the musical “The Sound of Music” children learn the scale with syllables.
Indian music has hundreds of different scales, called ragas, which suit particular times of day.

teile.einleitung: When you stretch, you deliberately lengthen muscles. It helps you stay flexible and is often part of training. It is important to do it calmly and in a controlled way.
wichtigste: In static stretching you hold a position for about 20 to 30 seconds.
Dynamic stretching uses controlled, swinging movements.
You should feel a slight pull, but no pain.
Heel to bottom stretches the front of the thigh.
In a lunge position with your heel on the ground you stretch the calf.
Jerky bouncing triggers a reflex and can lead to pulled muscles.

abschnitte.text: In **static stretching** you bring the muscle into a stretched position and hold it still. About **20 to 30 seconds** is typical. While doing this you keep breathing calmly. You should feel a **slight pull**. Pain is a warning signal, and then you ease off the stretch a little.

In **dynamic stretching** you move your arms or legs back and forth in a controlled way. One example is **leg swings** to the front and back. The movements slowly get bigger but always stay controlled. This form fits well into the **warm-up** because it prepares the body for fast movements. Static stretching, on the other hand, is often done after training.

If you pull your **heel to your bottom** while standing, your knee bends a lot. This stretches the four-headed **thigh muscle** (quadriceps) at the front. In a **lunge position** you press the heel of your back, straight leg onto the ground. This stretches the **calf muscle** at the back of the lower leg. You can hold on to a wall for support.

When stretching you should not **bounce jerkily**. Fast, jerky movements trigger the **stretch reflex**. Then the muscle contracts to protect itself instead of stretching. This can lead to **pulled muscles**. That is why you move calmly and in a controlled way when stretching.

gewusst: Many animals such as cats and dogs also stretch after sleeping.
The four-headed thigh muscle is one of the largest muscles in the body.

teile.einleitung: The time signature tells you how many beats a bar has and which note value makes one beat. It is written at the beginning of the music like a fraction, for example 3/4 or 4/4. From the time signature you can often already tell whether a piece is a waltz, a march or a pop song.
wichtigste: The time signature is written like a fraction at the beginning of the music.
The bottom number gives the note value of one beat, the top number the number of beats.
A bar of 3/4 has three crotchet beats and is typical of the waltz.
4/4 time is often written with the sign “C”.
Six quavers fit into a bar of 6/8.
The vertical line between the bars is called a barline.
An incomplete bar at the beginning of a piece is called an upbeat (anacrusis).

abschnitte.titel: How do you read a time signature?
abschnitte.text: The time signature looks like a fraction without the line. The **bottom number** shows the note value that counts as one beat: a 4 stands for crotchets (quarter notes) and an 8 for quavers (eighth notes). The **top number** shows how many of these beats fit into a bar. So a bar of 3/4 has three crotchet beats, a bar of 6/8 six quavers. Between the bars there are vertical **barlines**.

**4/4 time** is the most common time in pop, rock and many children's songs; it is often written simply with the sign “C”. 3/4 time is typical of the **waltz**, for example “The Blue Danube” by Johann Strauss (the son). 2/4 time suits marches and polkas well. A C with a line through it stands for alla breve time, in which you count in minims (half notes).

Every time signature has its own **stress pattern**. In 4/4 time the first beat is strongest and the third is stressed a little less. In 3/4 time you count “one, two, three”, and the “one” is heavy. 6/8 time is usually felt in two groups of three quavers; it sounds rocking, as in some lullabies.

Many songs do not begin with a whole bar but with a short run-up. This incomplete bar is called an **upbeat** (anacrusis). One example is “Happy Birthday”, in which the first two syllables “Hap-py” come before the first stressed beat. The last bar of a piece with an upbeat is usually shorter to match, so that the two together make a full bar.

There are also unusual time signatures such as 5/4 or 7/8. The famous jazz piece **“Take Five”** by the Dave Brubeck Quartet from 1959 is in 5/4 time. In the folk music of the Balkans irregular times such as 7/8 or 9/8 are quite normal. Some pieces even keep changing their time signature; this is called a **change of metre**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An indication of how many beats of which note value there are in a bar.
A vertical line that separates two bars.
An incomplete bar at the beginning of a piece.
A time signature in which you count in minims, written as a C with a line through it.

gewusst: The sign “C” for 4/4 time is not really a letter but a half circle from medieval musical notation.
In the Middle Ages triple time was considered perfect because the number three stood for the Holy Trinity.
When conducting, you draw a different pattern in the air for each time signature.

teile.einleitung: In competitive swimming there are four strokes: front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly. Each stroke has its own movements for the arms and legs and its own rules in competition.
wichtigste: The four competition strokes are freestyle (usually front crawl), backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly.
Front crawl is the fastest swimming stroke.
In the individual medley the order is butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, freestyle.
The medley relay starts with backstroke because that stroke starts in the water.
In butterfly both legs move at the same time like a dolphin's tail.
In breaststroke the legs make a whip kick like a frog.
Noè Ponti won Olympic bronze over 100 m butterfly in Tokyo in 2021.

abschnitte.text: In **front crawl** you lie on your front, your arms pull through the water one after the other and your legs kick quickly up and down. To breathe you turn your head to the side. In competition the event is called **freestyle** because you may swim any stroke. But almost everyone chooses front crawl because it is the fastest.

In **backstroke** you lie on your back and your face stays above the water. Your arms circle backwards one after the other, and your legs kick as in front crawl. It is the only competition stroke that starts **in the water**: you hold on to the starting block and push off from the wall. That is why the medley relay begins with backstroke.

Many children learn **breaststroke** as their first stroke. The arms pull out to the sides at the same time and come together again in front of the chest. The legs are drawn up, spread and snapped together powerfully. This **whip kick** is reminiscent of a frog. Breaststroke is the slowest competition stroke.

In **butterfly** both arms swing forwards over the water at the same time. The legs stay together and make the wave-like **dolphin kick**. That is why the stroke is also called **dolphin**. It needs a lot of strength and good technique. **Noè Ponti** from Ticino won Olympic bronze over 100 m butterfly in Tokyo in 2021.

In **medley swimming** all four strokes appear in one race. If one person swims alone, the order is **butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, freestyle**. In the **medley relay** four people swim one after the other: backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly, freestyle. So anyone who swims medley has to be good at all the strokes.

gewusst: The butterfly stroke developed from breaststroke and only became a separate competition stroke in the 1950s.
In freestyle you could even swim breaststroke, but it would be much slower than front crawl.

teile.einleitung: A World Championship, or World Cup in football, is a competition in which the best athletes or teams in the world decide who is world champion. There are world championships in almost every sport, from football to ski racing. The football World Cup is one of the biggest sporting events of all.
wichtigste: The first football World Cup took place in 1930, and Uruguay became world champion.
The 2026 football World Cup was hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico.
For the first time, 48 teams took part in the 2026 World Cup.
Spain won the 2026 football World Cup.
Brazil has the most men's World Cup titles.
Switzerland hosted the football World Cup in 1954.
The 2026 Ice Hockey World Championship took place in Zurich and Fribourg.

abschnitte.text: The men's football World Cup takes place every four years and is organised by **FIFA**. The first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay also became world champion. **Brazil** has won the most titles, namely five. The 2026 World Cup was hosted jointly by the USA, Canada and Mexico, with **48 teams** for the first time. Spain became world champion.

In 1954 Switzerland hosted the football World Cup. West Germany surprisingly won the final against Hungary in Bern's **Wankdorf Stadium**; people speak of the “Miracle of Bern”. In 2026 the men's **Ice Hockey World Championship** took place in Zurich and Fribourg. In 2027 the Alpine World Ski Championships will be held in **Crans-Montana** in Valais.

There are world championships in almost every sport, for example in athletics, swimming, alpine skiing, ice hockey and cycling. Some take place every year, others every two or four years. The Women's World Cup in football has existed since 1991. In cycling the world champion wears a white jersey with rainbow stripes for a year.

At big team world championships you first have to win a place in **qualifying**. At the tournament the teams first play in groups. The best go through to the **knockout stage**, where the loser is eliminated. Finally the world champion is decided in the final.

For many athletes a world title is the greatest success besides an Olympic medal. Football World Cups are watched on television by billions of people. For the host country they mean many visitors, but also high costs for stadiums and security. The Swiss national teams regularly take part in world championships.

begriffe.erklaerung: The world football federation, based in Zurich.
Elimination matches to win the right to take part in a tournament.
The phase of a tournament in which every loser is eliminated immediately.
The country in which a world championship takes place.

gewusst: The 2026 World Cup was the first to take place in three countries at the same time.
In 1954 the quarter-final between Switzerland and Austria, which ended 5 to 7, was the highest-scoring match in World Cup finals history, and it still is today.
The cycling world champion may wear the rainbow jersey for a year.

teile.einleitung: When skiing you glide over the snow on two long boards, the skis. In Switzerland skiing is a real national pastime, and many children learn it at ski school. There are very different kinds, from leisurely cross-country skiing to the high-speed downhill.
wichtigste: A helmet protects your head when skiing.
In Switzerland easy slopes are marked blue, medium ones red and difficult ones black.
The slalom has many tight turns around poles.
The downhill is the fastest discipline in alpine skiing.
Chairlifts and ski lifts take skiers up the mountain.
On the slopes the person further ahead always has priority.
Marco Odermatt won the overall World Cup every year from 2022 to 2026.

abschnitte.text: In **alpine skiing** you ski down the mountain on groomed slopes. In **cross-country skiing** you glide through the countryside in flat tracks, the trails. In ski touring you climb up the mountain yourself with skins under your skis. Freestyle skiers jump over kickers in the snow park and do tricks.

Alpine skiing has several disciplines. The **downhill** is the fastest, and professionals often reach over 130 kilometres per hour. In the super-G and the giant slalom the turns are tighter. The **slalom** has the most gates and the tightest turns around the poles. Famous races in Switzerland are the Lauberhorn race in Wengen and the races in Adelboden.

In Switzerland slopes are marked by colour: **blue** is easy, red medium and black difficult. Skiers get to the top with **chairlifts**, gondolas, cable cars or ski lifts. In 1934 one of the first T-bar lifts in the world was built in Davos. Piste bashers smooth the snow every night.

A **helmet** protects your head if you fall, together with ski goggles and warm clothing. The International Ski Federation has drawn up the **FIS rules** for behaviour on the slopes. The most important one: whoever is further ahead has priority, and whoever comes from behind must avoid them. You should only ski as fast as you can do safely. Away from the slopes there is a danger of avalanches.

**Marco Odermatt** from Nidwalden won the overall World Cup five times in a row from 2022 to 2026. Lara Gut-Behrami won the big crystal globe in 2016 and 2024. In cross-country skiing Dario Cologna won four Olympic gold medals. In 2027 the Alpine World Ski Championships will take place in Crans-Montana.

begriffe.erklaerung: A groomed run for skiers, marked with colours.
A prepared track for cross-country skiing.
Two poles through which or around which a racer must ski.
A skiing technique in which you draw clean arcs in the snow on the edge of your skis.

gewusst: The oldest skis in the world are several thousand years old and were found in Scandinavia and Russia.
At about 4.5 kilometres, the Lauberhorn downhill in Wengen is one of the longest in the world.
A World Cup skier is sometimes travelling faster than a car on the motorway.

teile.einleitung: The violin, also called the fiddle, is a string instrument with four strings. You draw a bow across the strings and hold the instrument between your chin and shoulder. The violin is the highest instrument of the string family and often plays the melody in the orchestra.
wichtigste: Violin and fiddle are two names for the same instrument.
A violin has four strings.
You draw a bow across the strings.
The bow is traditionally strung with horsehair.
So that the bow grips well, you rub rosin on the hairs.
When playing, you hold the violin between your chin and shoulder.
The cello looks like a large violin and stands on the floor when played.

abschnitte.text: The **body** of the violin is a hollow wooden box that amplifies the sound. The top is usually made of spruce, the back and sides of maple. In the top there are two sound holes shaped like an f, the **f-holes**. The four strings run over a small wooden bridge and are tuned at the pegs at the top. The upper end is carved into an elaborate **scroll**.

The **bow** consists of a wooden stick and a ribbon of horsehair. So that the hairs grip the strings and make them vibrate, you rub them with **rosin**, a substance made from tree resin. Without rosin the bow would hardly make any sound. You can also pluck the strings with your finger; this is called **pizzicato**.

The four strings of the violin are tuned to the notes G, D, A and E. With the fingers of your left hand you press the strings onto the fingerboard and so change the pitch. Your right hand guides the bow. Because the violin has no frets like a guitar, you have to find exactly the right spot. For children there are smaller violins, for example in quarter or half sizes.

The violin is the smallest and highest instrument of the **string family**. A little larger and lower is the viola. The **cello** is much larger and stands on the floor when played. The double bass sounds lowest. In the orchestra the strings form the largest group.

The violin appeared in the 16th century in northern Italy. In the town of Cremona masters such as **Antonio Stradivari** built violins that are worth millions today. The Italian Niccolò Paganini was a world-famous violinist in the 19th century. In Switzerland there is a violin-making school in **Brienz**, where you can learn the trade of violin maker.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument whose strings are played with a bow.
A resin that is rubbed on the bow hairs so that they grip the strings.
Plucking the strings with the finger instead of using the bow.
A craftsperson who builds and repairs violins and other string instruments.
The long black board onto which you press the strings with your fingers.

gewusst: A violin consists of about 70 separate wooden parts.
A single violin bow needs about 150 to 200 horsehairs.
Today a violin by Antonio Stradivari is often worth more than a house.

teile.einleitung: The basketball rules set out how the game is played, how points are counted and what is not allowed. Internationally the rules of the world federation FIBA apply; in the American NBA there are some differences. Many rules make sure the game stays fast and fair.
wichtigste: Each team has five players on the court at the same time.
The basket hangs exactly 3.05 metres high.
A basket from outside the three-point line counts 3 points.
A team has 24 seconds to shoot at the basket.
Under FIBA rules a game lasts 4 times 10 minutes.
After five personal fouls a player has to leave the game.
Anyone who takes too many steps with the ball commits travelling.

abschnitte.text: A game under **FIBA rules** consists of four quarters of 10 minutes each. In the NBA a quarter lasts 12 minutes. If the score is level at the end of playing time, there is **overtime** of 5 minutes, repeated until one team wins. Only actual playing time is counted; the clock stops during interruptions. The court is 28 metres long and 15 metres wide, and the basket hangs at 3.05 metres.

A basket during play counts 2 points, and behind the **three-point line** you get 3 points. Under FIBA rules this line is 6.75 metres from the basket. A **free throw** counts 1 point and is taken from the free-throw line without interference. If a player is fouled during an unsuccessful three-point shot, they get three free throws.

With the ball in your hand you may take at most two steps. If you take more, that is **travelling**, and the opponents get the ball. Anyone who has stopped dribbling may not start dribbling again; otherwise it is a **double dribble**. You may not play the ball with your foot or punch it with your fist.

A team has **24 seconds** to shoot at the basket, and a big clock above the basket shows the time left. The ball must be brought from your own half into the opponents' half within 8 seconds. An attacker may stay in the **key** (the restricted area) under the opponents' basket for at most 3 seconds. These rules stop a team from just holding on to the ball.

Basketball is meant to be a non-contact game: pushing, holding and hitting are not allowed. Every rule break involving body contact is a **foul**. Under FIBA rules a player has to leave the game after five personal fouls, in the NBA only after six. If a team has already committed four fouls in a quarter, every further foul gives the opponents free throws.

begriffe.erklaerung: The international basketball federation, which sets the rules.
Taking too many steps with the ball in your hand without dribbling.
Dribbling again after you have already held the ball with both hands.
The marked area under the basket in which attackers may stay for only 3 seconds.
Body contact with an opponent that is not allowed.

gewusst: The 24-second rule was introduced in the NBA in 1954 because games had sometimes been very boring before.
The basket height of 3.05 metres equals exactly 10 feet and dates back to the very first game in 1891.
The three-point line has only existed in the FIBA rules since 1984.

teile.einleitung: Some sporting events are so special that they have gone down in history. They show magnificent achievements, but sometimes also how closely sport is linked to politics. Some of these events even took place in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Pierre de Coubertin is regarded as the founder of the modern Olympic Games.
The first Olympic Winter Games took place in Chamonix in 1924.
In 1954 West Germany won the World Cup final against Hungary in Bern's Wankdorf Stadium.
Jesse Owens won four gold medals in Berlin in 1936.
In 1954 Roger Bannister became the first person to run a mile in under 4 minutes.
Uruguay won the first football World Cup in 1930.
In 2003 the Swiss team Alinghi became the first European team to win the America's Cup.

abschnitte.titel: A new start for the Olympic Games
abschnitte.text: The Frenchman **Pierre de Coubertin** wanted to revive the Games of ancient times. In 1896 the first Olympic Games of modern times took place in **Athens**. In 1924 the first Olympic Winter Games followed in **Chamonix** in France. Switzerland hosted the Winter Games twice, with St Moritz in 1928 and 1948.

In 1930 the first football World Cup took place in **Uruguay**, and the host country won it. In 1954 Switzerland hosted the World Cup. In the final in Bern's **Wankdorf Stadium**, West Germany beat the favourites Hungary 3 to 2. In Germany this victory is still called the **“Miracle of Bern”** today.

On 6 May 1954 the Briton **Roger Bannister** became the first person to run a mile in under 4 minutes, in Oxford. Many had previously thought this impossible. In 1976 the 14-year-old gymnast **Nadia Comăneci** in Montreal was the first to be awarded a score of 10.0 at the Olympic Games. In 1968 Bob Beamon jumped 8.90 metres in Mexico City, so far that the record lasted for over 20 years.

In 1936 the Olympic Games took place in Berlin, and the Nazis used them for their propaganda. The black American **Jesse Owens** won four gold medals there. In 1972 in Munich, Palestinian terrorists took members of the Israeli team hostage, and eleven Israeli athletes and coaches were killed. In 1980 and 1984 many countries boycotted the Games in Moscow and Los Angeles because of the Cold War.

The **America's Cup** is one of the oldest sporting trophies in the world; it has been awarded in sailing since 1851. In 2003 the team **Alinghi** of the Swiss businessman Ernesto Bertarelli won the cup ahead of New Zealand. It was the first time a European team had won. This was particularly astonishing because Switzerland has no access to the sea at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest sporting festival in the world, held every four years in summer and in winter.
When countries deliberately do not take part as a protest.
The best performance ever measured anywhere in the world in an event.
A famous trophy for sailing races, awarded since 1851.
The surprising German World Cup victory in Bern in 1954.

gewusst: Roger Bannister was a medical student and often trained only during his lunch break.
Roger Bannister's record was beaten after only 46 days.
Alinghi successfully defended the America's Cup in Valencia in 2007.

teile.einleitung: Media effects research studies what newspapers, television, social media and other media do to us. It asks, for example, whether news changes our opinions or whether watching a lot of television makes us more fearful. The answers are often surprising and much less simple than you might think.
wichtigste: Media effects research is part of communication science.
Agenda-setting theory says that the media mainly decide what we think about.
According to George Gerbner's cultivation hypothesis, heavy viewers think the world is more dangerous than it is.
Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann developed the theory of the spiral of silence.
The uses and gratifications approach asks what people do with media.
Gatekeepers decide which news is published at all.
Fans can build up a one-sided, parasocial relationship with influencers.

abschnitte.text: Researchers want to know how media influence people's knowledge, feelings, opinions and behaviour. To find out, they carry out **surveys**, observe people or do experiments. For example, they compare what appears in the news with what people think is important. In the past it was believed that media worked like an injection, affecting everyone directly in the same way. Today we know that each person takes in media differently.

Around 1970 in the USA the researchers Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw showed that the media set the topics. This is called **agenda-setting**: the media tell us less about what we should think, but very much about what we think about. Who decides which topics get into the newspaper? The **gatekeepers**, such as editorial teams. Today the algorithms of platforms such as TikTok or YouTube also play a role like this.

abschnitte.titel: Cultivation and the spiral of silence
abschnitte.text: From the 1960s the American George Gerbner studied people who watch a great deal of television. His **cultivation hypothesis** says that heavy viewers think the world is more dangerous because so many crimes are shown on television. In the 1970s the German researcher Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann described the **spiral of silence**. Anyone who believes their opinion is in the minority is more likely to stay silent. As a result, this opinion seems even rarer than it really is.

As early as the 1940s Paul Lazarsfeld found that many people get information not directly from the media but from people they know. In the **two-step flow**, opinion leaders pass on media content and interpret it. The **uses and gratifications approach** turns the question around: what do people do with media? For example, people watch series to relax, news to get information or videos so that they can join in conversations.

In 1964 the Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan wrote the famous sentence “The medium is the message”. He meant that the type of medium itself changes our lives, no matter what is broadcast. Today social media, influencers and filter bubbles are also studied. Many fans feel close to their favourite stars even though the stars do not know them at all. This one-sided bond is called a **parasocial relationship**.

In Switzerland communication science is taught at universities including Zurich, Fribourg and Lugano. Every year the University of Zurich publishes the **Yearbook on the Quality of the Media**. The ZHAW in Winterthur uses the JAMES study to examine how young people in Switzerland use media. Studies like this show, for example, how many hours teenagers spend on their mobile phones.

begriffe.erklaerung: The media decide which topics seem important to us.
A person or editorial team that chooses which news is published.
Anyone who feels in the minority voices their opinion less often.
A person who explains media content to others and passes it on.
A one-sided friendship that you have with a star only in your mind.

gewusst: The term parasocial relationship has existed since 1956, long before Instagram and YouTube.
Since 2010 the JAMES study has shown every two years how Swiss teenagers use mobile phones, the internet and games.
Marshall McLuhan also coined the expression “global village” for a world closely connected by media.

teile.einleitung: Athletics is a collection of sports involving running, jumping and throwing. It is one of the oldest sports in the world and forms the core of the Olympic Games. From the 100 metres to the marathon, it measures who is fastest, who gets highest or who reaches furthest.
wichtigste: Athletics includes running, jumping, throwing and combined events.
One lap of the running track in a stadium is 400 metres long.
A marathon is just over 42 kilometres long.
In a relay race you pass a baton to the next runner.
In the pole vault you jump over a bar with a long pole.
The men's 100 metres world record is held by Usain Bolt (as of 2026).
The Weltklasse Zürich meeting takes place in Zurich every year.

abschnitte.text: In running a distinction is made between **sprints** such as the 100, 200 and 400 metres, middle distances such as the 800 and 1500 metres, and long distances. The longest distance is the **marathon** at 42.195 kilometres. In a **relay race** four runners run one after the other and pass on a baton. In hurdle races obstacles have to be jumped. One lap of the stadium measures 400 metres.

There are four jumping events: the long jump, triple jump, high jump and **pole vault**. In the long jump you land in a **sandpit**, where the distance is measured. In the high jump most athletes today jump over the bar backwards; this technique is called the Fosbury flop. In the pole vault you swing yourself over six metres high with a flexible pole.

The throwing events include the shot put, discus, javelin and hammer. In **combined events** athletes have to be good at many disciplines. Men usually compete in the **decathlon**, women in the heptathlon; both last two days. The winner is whoever collects the most points in total.

There was already a stadium race at the ancient Olympic Games in 776 BC. Athletics has been part of the modern Olympic Games since 1896. In Berlin in 2009 the Jamaican **Usain Bolt** ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, a world record that still stands today (as of 2026). Since 2019 the world federation has been called **World Athletics**, and it is based in Monaco.

The **Weltklasse Zürich** meeting in the Letzigrund stadium is one of the best-known athletics events in the world. The sprinter **Mujinga Kambundji** became European champion over 200 metres in 2022. Her sister Ditaji Kambundji is a successful hurdler. Werner Günthör was world champion in the shot put three times in the 1980s and 1990s. Many children gain their first experience in an athletics club or at the school sports day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short, very fast race, for example over 100 metres.
A race in which several runners run one after the other and pass on a baton.
A competition made up of ten athletics events over two days.
A high-jump technique in which you jump over the bar backwards.
An athletics event with many competitions.

gewusst: The Fosbury flop is named after the American Dick Fosbury, who became Olympic champion with it in 1968.
Many world records have been set at Weltklasse Zürich.
A men's shot weighs 7.26 kilograms, about as much as seven litres of water.

teile.einleitung: Lactate is produced in the body when sugar is broken down without enough oxygen. In sport the lactate level in the blood is measured to assess endurance. But lactate is not simply a waste product; it is also used again for energy.
wichtigste: Lactate is the salt of lactic acid.
At rest the blood lactate level is about 1 mmol/l.
The classic threshold according to Mader is 4 mmol/l.
For a lactate test a drop of blood from the earlobe or fingertip is enough.
In the liver lactate is turned back into glucose in the Cori cycle.
Lactate is constantly produced and broken down even at rest.

abschnitte.text: Chemically, **lactate** is the salt of **lactic acid**. In the body, lactic acid is almost entirely present as lactate. It is produced when glucose is broken down **anaerobically**, that is without enough oxygen. Even at rest, the red blood cells, for example, constantly produce lactate. What matters is the **balance** between production and breakdown.

At rest the lactate level in the blood is usually about **0.5 to 2 mmol/l**, so roughly 1 mmol/l. During hard exercise it rises. During maximum efforts it can rise to over **20 mmol/l**. According to the model of **Alois Mader**, the aerobic-anaerobic threshold is set at **4 mmol/l**. For individuals, however, this threshold can differ considerably.

In **lactate testing** you run or cycle a **step test** in which the effort keeps increasing. After each step a small drop of capillary blood is taken, usually from the **earlobe** or the **fingertip**. The values are plotted against speed or power. This gives the **lactate performance curve**. If it shifts to the right, endurance has improved.

Lactate travels in the blood to the **liver**. There it is turned back into glucose through **gluconeogenesis**, and this glucose can return to the muscles. This cycle is called the **Cori cycle**. The **heart** and muscles with a good blood supply also use lactate as fuel. That is why the lactate level falls faster during an easy **cool-down jog** than at complete rest.

gewusst: The Cori cycle is named after the married researchers Carl and Gerty Cori, who received the Nobel Prize in 1947.
For a long time people believed lactate was to blame for muscle soreness. Today we know that it is mainly caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres.

teile.einleitung: The Chinese remainder theorem is a mathematical theorem about remainders in division. It says that you can work out an unknown number exactly if you know its remainders when it is divided by several suitable numbers. A famous puzzle about it comes from an old Chinese arithmetic book: which number leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, a remainder of 3 when divided by 5 and a remainder of 2 when divided by 7? The answer is 23.
wichtigste: The Chinese remainder theorem is about remainders in division.
It comes from a Chinese maths book that is over 1500 years old.
The classic example is the number 23.
23 divided by 3 leaves a remainder of 2, by 5 a remainder of 3 and by 7 a remainder of 2.
The divisors must have no common factor except 1.
The solution always repeats after the product of the divisors, here after 105.
Today the theorem is used, for example, in encrypting data.

abschnitte.text: If you divide 23 by 5, the 5 goes in four times, which makes 20, and 3 are left over. This 3 is the **remainder**. The remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by. Working with remainders is also called **modulo arithmetic**, as on a clock, where 1 comes again after 12.

The famous puzzle appears in the book **Sunzi Suanjing**, a Chinese maths book probably written between the 3rd and 5th centuries. It asks for exactly the number that leaves the remainders 2, 3 and 2 when divided by 3, 5 and 7. Later, in the 13th century, the Chinese mathematician Qin Jiushao described a general method. In Europe, **Carl Friedrich Gauss** proved the theorem in 1801 in his famous book on number theory.

First you look for numbers that leave a remainder of 2 when divided both by 3 and by 7. These are 2, 23, 44, 65 and 86; they are always 21 apart. Now you check which of them leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 5. That is **23**, and between 1 and 100 it is the only solution.

The divisors must be **coprime**, which means they have no common factor except 1. That is true of 3, 5 and 7. Then there is always a solution, and it is unique if you look only at numbers up to the **product** of the divisors. Here that is 3 times 5 times 7, which is 105, so the next solution would be 128.

The Chinese remainder theorem is used in **cryptography**, for example in the RSA encryption method, which protects online banking and messages. With its help, computers can split very large numbers into smaller parts and calculate faster. Remainder problems like this also turn up in calendar calculations. And it is a popular brain teaser in maths competitions.

begriffe.erklaerung: What is left over in a division that does not work out exactly.
Two numbers that have no common factor except 1.
Arithmetic in which only the remainder after division counts.
The science of encrypting messages.

gewusst: You can do a magic trick with the remainder theorem: if someone tells you the remainders of a number they are thinking of when divided by 3, 5 and 7, you can guess their number up to 105.
The theorem only got the name “Chinese remainder theorem” much later, from European mathematicians.

teile.einleitung: Sports economics deals with the money in sport: ticket sales, broadcasting rights, sponsors and players' wages. Today big sporting events and professional leagues involve billions. Clubs, sports shops and manufacturers of sporting goods are part of it too.
wichtigste: The Bosman ruling of 1995 made free transfers at the end of a contract possible within the EU.
UEFA's Financial Fair Play was adopted in 2010.
North American professional leagues have a limit on wages, the salary cap.
The IOC's biggest source of income is the sale of broadcasting rights.
Ambush marketing is advertising at a major event without official sponsorship rights.
In 2017 Neymar moved for 222 million euros, the highest transfer fee so far.
The Football Money League divides income into matchday, broadcasting and commercial.

abschnitte.text: Professional clubs earn money in three big areas; this is how the **Football Money League** of the firm Deloitte divides it. They include **matchday** income, such as tickets and food, then **broadcasting rights** for television and the internet, and **commercial** income from sponsors and merchandise. One example: a stadium with 30 000 seats that is 80 per cent full brings in 960 000 francs at an average price of 40 francs. For the IOC the sale of broadcasting rights is the biggest source of income.

The Belgian footballer Jean-Marc Bosman took legal action against the transfer rules of the time. In 1995 the **European Court of Justice** ruled in his favour. Since then players can move on a free transfer within the EU at the end of their contract. The ruling changed European football a great deal because the players gained more power. The current record for transfer fees is held by Neymar, who moved to Paris in 2017 for 222 million euros.

In 2010 UEFA adopted **Financial Fair Play**. Clubs are not supposed to spend more than they earn in the long run. In North American leagues such as the NFL there is a limit on wages, the **salary cap**. In the **draft**, the weakest team of the previous season is normally allowed to choose a young player first. This is meant to keep the leagues balanced and exciting.

Companies pay a lot of money for their name to appear on shirts, advertising boards or stadiums. Official sponsors of the Olympics or a World Cup have special rights. If a company attaches itself to a major event without these rights, it is called **ambush marketing**. In Germany the **50+1 rule** says that the parent club must keep the majority of votes in its professional section.

Many international sports federations have their headquarters in Switzerland, for example the IOC in Lausanne, FIFA in Zurich and UEFA in Nyon. They bring jobs and visitors to the country. Winter tourism in the ski resorts is also an important industry. Well-known Swiss sporting goods companies include the running shoe maker On from Zurich and Mammut for mountain sports equipment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money a club pays to take a player out of an existing contract.
A company that supports sport with money and gets advertising in return.
Permission to show a sporting event on television or the internet.
An upper limit on a team's wages.

gewusst: Neymar's transfer fee was more than twice as high as the previous record.
There are so many sports federations around Lake Geneva that the region is sometimes called the “sports capital of the world”.
In the NFL draft, players are usually chosen straight from American universities.

teile.einleitung: Sports medicine is a field of medicine that looks after the health of athletes. It helps to prevent, recognise and properly treat injuries. It also studies how exercise keeps the body healthy.
wichtigste: For acute sports injuries the PECH rule helps: rest (Pause), ice (Eis), compression, elevation (Hochlagern).
The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin bone from sliding forwards.
The medical term for concussion is commotio cerebri.
An AED is an automated external defibrillator for heart emergencies.
Muscle soreness is caused by tiny tears in the muscle fibres.
When the core body temperature is over 40 °C, it is called heatstroke.
Stress fractures are caused by repeated overload.

abschnitte.text: For bruises, strains and sprains the **PECH rule** helps (in English it is often called RICE). P stands for Pause (rest), E for Eis (ice) for cooling, C for **compression**, meaning a pressure bandage, and H for Hochlagern (elevation). This way the injured area swells less. If the pain is severe or something looks out of place, you must see a doctor.

When you twist your ankle over the outer edge of your foot, a **supination injury**, it is usually the outer ligaments of the ankle joint that are injured. In the knee, the **anterior cruciate ligament** often tears during twisting movements, for example when skiing or playing football. It stops the shin bone from sliding forwards in relation to the thigh bone. The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone and can tear when overloaded.

Some problems are not caused by an accident but by too much strain. The medical name for **tennis elbow** is lateral epicondylitis, and it is an irritation of the tendons at the elbow. A **stress fracture** is a broken bone caused by repeated overload, for example in runners. Muscle soreness is caused by tiny tears in the muscle fibres and goes away by itself after a few days.

Concussion, **commotio cerebri**, can be caused by a blow to the head. Headache, nausea and dizziness are typical, and you must then definitely rest. In a sudden cardiac arrest an **AED**, an automated external defibrillator, can save lives. It gives an electric shock and tells you exactly what to do with a voice. In Switzerland you dial 144 in an emergency.

In great heat there is a risk of **heatstroke** if the core body temperature rises above 40 °C. That is why you should drink enough and train less hard when it is hot. Warming up, good shoes and protective equipment such as helmets help to prevent injuries. Sports doctors also examine athletes regularly, for example with an exercise test.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rest, ice, compression, elevation: first aid for sports injuries (in English often RICE).
A strong ligament in the knee that firmly connects the thigh and the lower leg.
A device that helps with an electric shock in cardiac arrest.
A broken bone caused by constant overload rather than a single accident.

gewusst: An AED is built so that even untrained members of the public can use it.
