A device with buttons that you hold in your hand to control the game.
A setting with which parents limit playing time and games.

gewusst: From 1889 Nintendo sold hand-painted hanafuda playing cards, long before video games existed.
One Game Boy survived a bomb attack in the 1991 Gulf War and still worked afterwards.
The first home console, the Magnavox Odyssey, had no sound and used plastic overlays that were stuck onto the screen.

teile.einleitung: Muscles are made of many long, thin cells, the muscle fibres. There are slow fibres for endurance and fast fibres for strength and speed. Which fibres someone has influences what they are particularly talented at in sport.
wichtigste: Slow-twitch type I fibres are reddish because they contain a lot of myoglobin.
Fast-twitch type II fibres are powerful but tire quickly.
Type IIa fibres are a mixed type and become more enduring through endurance training.
A motor neuron and its fibres form a motor unit.
Marathon runners have especially many type I fibres in their legs.
Strength training makes the fibres thicker: hypertrophy.

abschnitte.text: **Type I fibres** contract slowly but hardly get tired. They contain a lot of **myoglobin**, a red pigment that stores oxygen. That is why they are also called **red fibres**. They get their energy mainly with the help of oxygen. **Marathon runners** often have well over half of these fibres in their calf muscles.

**Type II fibres** contract quickly and powerfully. They get much of their energy **anaerobically** and therefore tire quickly. Sprinters and throwers have especially many of them. **Type IIa fibres** are a **mixed type**: they are fast but also have a good aerobic capacity. They change their properties particularly clearly through training.

Each muscle fibre is controlled by a nerve cell, a **motor neuron**. A motor neuron and all the fibres it supplies form a **motor unit**. All the fibres of a unit belong to the same type. According to Henneman's **size principle**, when little force is needed the small units with type I fibres work first. Only when more force is needed do the large units with type II fibres join in.

The proportion of fibre types can be determined with a **muscle biopsy**. A small sample of tissue is taken, stained and counted under the microscope. **Strength training** makes the fibres thicker because they store more proteins. This is called **hypertrophy**. The opposite, muscle wasting, is called **atrophy**.

gewusst: In chickens the breast meat is pale and the leg meat darker, because there are more enduring red fibres there.
A single muscle fibre can be several centimetres long.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a small country, but it has produced many world-class athletes. Especially in skiing, tennis and cycling, Swiss athletes keep celebrating big victories. Some of them, like Roger Federer, are famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slam singles titles during his career.
Simon Ammann won four Olympic gold medals in ski jumping.
Dario Cologna won four Olympic gold medals in cross-country skiing.
By 2026 Marco Odermatt had won the overall alpine skiing World Cup five times in a row.
Lara Gut-Behrami won the overall World Cup in 2016 and 2024.
Belinda Bencic became Olympic singles tennis champion in Tokyo in 2021.
Ditaji Kambundji became world champion over the 100 metres hurdles in Tokyo in 2025.

abschnitte.text: **Roger Federer** from Basel won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, eight of them at the famous tournament at Wimbledon. He ended his career in 2022. **Martina Hingis** became world number 1 in 1997 at the age of just 16. Stan Wawrinka won three Grand Slam tournaments. Belinda Bencic won singles gold at the Olympic Games in Tokyo in 2021.

**Marco Odermatt** from Nidwalden won the overall alpine skiing World Cup five times in a row from 2022 to 2026. **Lara Gut-Behrami** from Ticino won the big crystal globe in 2016 and 2024. In earlier years Vreni Schneider and Pirmin Zurbriggen were big skiing stars. Simon Ammann won two Olympic golds in **ski jumping** in both 2002 and 2010. Dario Cologna from Val Müstair won at the Olympics four times in cross-country skiing.

**Nino Schurter** from the Grisons became Olympic **mountain bike** champion in Rio de Janeiro in 2016. He has also been world champion many times and is regarded as one of the best mountain bikers of all time. Fabian Cancellara from Bern won Olympic gold in the road time trial in 2008 and 2016. Cycling is very popular in Switzerland, for example at the Tour de Suisse.

**Ditaji Kambundji** from Bern became world champion over the **100 metres hurdles** in Tokyo in 2025. Her older sister Mujinga Kambundji is one of the best sprinters in Europe. Athletics is getting more and more attention in Switzerland. A well-known meeting is “Weltklasse Zürich” in the Letzigrund stadium.

In **Schwingen** (Swiss wrestling) strong men and women compete in sawdust. The winner of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival is called the **Schwingerkönig** (wrestling king). Switzerland is also strong in ice hockey, floorball and curling. Many athletes are supported by the Federal Office of Sport in Magglingen.

begriffe.erklaerung: The four most important tennis tournaments in the world.
The ranking over a whole ski season; the winner receives the big crystal globe.
Someone who wins gold at the Olympic Games.
The winner of the big Federal Wrestling Festival.

gewusst: In 2002 Simon Ammann became famous so suddenly with his double victory that people compared him to Harry Potter.
Roger Federer won the tournament in his home town of Basel, the Swiss Indoors, ten times.
In 2022 in Beijing Marco Odermatt also became Olympic giant slalom champion.

teile.einleitung: The history of film tells how moving pictures became the cinema we know today. It begins in 1895 with the first film screenings in Paris and stretches from silent films, talkies and colour films to digital cinema. Switzerland also has its place in it, with the Locarno Film Festival and an Oscar.
wichtigste: In 1895 the Lumière brothers showed films to a paying audience in Paris for the first time.
A classic cinema film shows 24 single pictures per second.
In 1902 Georges Méliès made “A Trip to the Moon”.
Charlie Chaplin became famous as the Tramp with a bowler hat and walking stick.
“The Jazz Singer” from 1927 is regarded as the first feature film with spoken dialogue passages.
The Oscars were presented for the first time in 1929.
The Swiss film “Journey of Hope” by Xavier Koller won an Oscar in 1991.
The Locarno Film Festival takes place on the Piazza Grande in Ticino.

abschnitte.text: A film consists of many single pictures that are shown so quickly one after the other that the eye sees **movement**. A classic cinema film shows **24 pictures per second**. On 28 December 1895 the brothers **Auguste and Louis Lumière** showed films to a paying audience in Paris for the first time. Their device was called the cinematograph and was a camera and projector in one. One of their first films showed workers leaving a factory.

abschnitte.titel: Trick artists and silent film stars
abschnitte.text: The French magician **Georges Méliès** invented many film tricks and in 1902 made “A Trip to the Moon”, in which a rocket lands in the eye of the Moon. In the **silent film era** there was no sound yet; musicians played live in the cinema. The Briton **Charlie Chaplin** became a world star as the Tramp with a bowler hat and walking stick. In Germany Fritz Lang made “Metropolis” in 1927, about a huge city of the future with a machine-human. During this time **Hollywood**, a district of Los Angeles, became the centre of the American film industry.

In 1927 “**The Jazz Singer**” came to the cinema; it is regarded as the first feature film with synchronised spoken dialogue passages. Within a few years **sound films** replaced silent films, and some silent film stars lost their careers. In 1929 the **Oscars** were presented in Hollywood for the first time. In the 1930s colour films made with the Technicolor process became popular, for example “The Wizard of Oz” from 1939. In 1937 Walt Disney also brought out a long colour cartoon, “Snow White”.

From the 1950s cinema faced competition from **television**. The film studios responded with wide screens, splendid colour films and lavish spectacles. In the 1970s the first big **blockbusters** appeared, such as “Jaws” and “Star Wars”. Later came video cassettes and DVDs, with which people could watch films at home. In 1995 “Toy Story” came out, the first cinema film animated entirely on the computer.

Since about 2010 most cinemas have shown films **digitally** instead of playing them from reels of film. Today special effects are often created entirely on the computer. With **streaming services** many people watch new films straight at home. Even so, a great many people around the world still go to the cinema to experience films on the big screen. With Bollywood, India produces especially many films every year.

The **Locarno Film Festival** in the canton of Ticino has existed since 1946. On the **Piazza Grande**, thousands of people watch films under the open sky on a huge screen every August. In 1991 the director **Xavier Koller** won the Oscar for best foreign-language film with “Journey of Hope”. The film tells of a Turkish family who want to flee to Switzerland. Other important meeting points are the Solothurn Film Festival and the Zurich Film Festival.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Lumière brothers' device, which could both film and show films.
A film without sound from the early days of cinema.
A film in which speech, music and noises can be heard.
A very expensive and very successful cinema film.
The most famous film award in the world, presented in Hollywood.

gewusst: According to a legend, viewers of an early Lumière film were frightened by a train arriving at a station, but whether this is true is disputed.
The screen on the Piazza Grande in Locarno is one of the largest open-air screens in Europe.
Charlie Chaplin spent the last years of his life in Corsier-sur-Vevey on Lake Geneva, where the museum Chaplin's World remembers him today.

teile.einleitung: At 828 metres, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the tallest building in the world (as of 2026). It opened in 2010 and rises like a silver needle out of the desert city in the United Arab Emirates. The tower is more than four times as tall as the tallest building in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Burj Khalifa is 828 metres tall.
It is the tallest building in the world (as of 2026).
It stands in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates.
It opened on 4 January 2010.
It has over 160 floors.
It is named after Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the Emirates at the time.
The tower contains flats, offices, a hotel and viewing platforms.

abschnitte.text: The **Burj Khalifa** stands in the Downtown Dubai district of the **United Arab Emirates**. At 828 metres it is almost three times as tall as the Eiffel Tower. It has over 160 floors, which are reached with very fast lifts. “Burj” means “tower” in Arabic.

Building began in 2004 and took about six years. It was designed by the architect **Adrian Smith** of the American firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill. The shape with three wings is inspired by a desert flower and makes the tower stable against the **wind**. Towards the top the tower gets narrower step by step and ends in a slender steel spire.

The Burj Khalifa contains luxury flats, offices and a hotel. The **viewing platform** “At the Top” is on the 124th and 125th floors, and an even higher one is on the 148th floor at about 555 metres. In clear weather you can see far across the desert and the sea. At the foot of the tower lies the **Dubai Fountain**, a huge display of dancing water with music.

The tower holds several records, for example for the tallest building and the structure with the most floors. Before it, Taipei 101 in Taiwan was the tallest building in the world. In Saudi Arabia the **Jeddah Tower** is being built, which is meant to be over 1000 metres tall. Until it is finished, however, the Burj Khalifa stays at the top (as of 2026).

The tallest building in Switzerland is Roche’s **Building 2** in Basel, at 205 metres. So the Burj Khalifa is a good four times as tall. For comparison: the Uetliberg near Zurich is around 870 metres above sea level, roughly as high as the tower is tall. In Dubai it gets hotter than 40 degrees in summer, which is why the **concrete** often had to be poured at night and cooled with ice during construction.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very tall building with many floors.
A place high up from which you can see a long way.
A state or area ruled by an emir.
A person who plans and designs buildings.

gewusst: At the very top of the tower it is several degrees cooler than on the ground.
The windows of the Burj Khalifa are cleaned by workers hanging on ropes and machines on the outside of the building.

teile.einleitung: Sport psychology studies what goes on in athletes' heads. It deals with motivation, concentration, nerves and coping with pressure. In sport it is not only the body that decides between victory and defeat, but often the mind too.
wichtigste: Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoying the activity itself.
The Yerkes-Dodson law says that a medium level of arousal brings the best performance.
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described the experience of flow.
Albert Bandura coined the term self-efficacy.
Choking means suddenly failing under high pressure.
In 1898 Norman Triplett showed that people are faster when others are present.
In SMART goals the M stands for measurable.

abschnitte.text: **Motivation** is the inner drive to do something. It is called **intrinsic motivation** when it comes from enjoying the activity itself. Extrinsic motivation comes from rewards from outside, such as prizes, money or praise. People who do sport for enjoyment usually stick with it longer. The psychologist Albert Bandura coined the term **self-efficacy**, meaning confidence that you can manage a task through your own efforts.

The **Yerkes-Dodson law** describes an inverted U-shaped relationship between arousal and performance. If you are too relaxed, you perform poorly, but the same is true if you are too worked up. A medium level of tension is best. Suddenly failing under high pressure despite good skills is called **choking**, for example a missed penalty at the decisive moment.

The psychologist **Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi** described the experience of **flow**. In this state you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time. Flow happens when a task is neither too easy nor too difficult. Many athletes report that they produced their best performances in this state.

In 1898 Norman Triplett studied racing cyclists and found that people are faster when others are present. This is regarded as one of the first experiments in social psychology. The **Ringelmann effect** shows the opposite: in a group, individuals often achieve less than when alone. It was first observed in **tug of war**. According to Bernard Weiner's attribution theory, luck or chance counts as an external and changeable cause of success.

In **mental training** athletes imagine movements precisely in their minds. According to the **Carpenter effect**, merely imagining a movement can trigger measurable muscle activity. Ski racers, for example, go through the whole course with their eyes closed before the start. Clear goals using the SMART formula also help: specific, measurable, attractive, realistic and time-bound.

begriffe.erklaerung: Coming from within, out of your own enjoyment.
A state in which you are completely absorbed in an activity.
Failing under great pressure even though you can actually do it.
Confidence in your own abilities.
Practising movements and sequences in your imagination.

gewusst: Triplett's study from 1898 is regarded as one of the very first experiments in social psychology.
Today many top athletes work with their own sport psychologist.
In tug of war, eight people pulling together pull less than eight times as hard as one person alone.

teile.einleitung: Skipping is a simple game and at the same time a real sport. All you need is a rope and a little space. As a competitive sport with tricks it is called rope skipping.
wichtigste: A skipping rope of the right length reaches to just below your armpits when you stand on the middle of it.
You turn the rope mainly from your wrists.
You land softly on the balls of your feet.
In a double under the rope passes under your feet twice.
In a cross jump you cross your arms in front of your body.
In Double Dutch you jump over two ropes turning in opposite directions.
Skipping trains endurance and coordination.

abschnitte.text: A rope must suit your height. You stand with both feet on the **middle of the rope** and pull the handles up. If they reach roughly **to just below your armpits**, the rope is the right length. A rope that is too short catches on your feet, and one that is too long drags on the ground.

The rope is turned mainly from the **wrists**, and your arms stay close to your body. You jump only as high as necessary and land softly on the **balls of your feet**. This cushions the jump and protects your joints. You look straight ahead and keep your upper body upright.

Once you can do the basic jump, you can try tricks. In a **cross jump** you cross your arms in front of your body, and the rope forms a loop that you jump through. In a **double under** you jump so high that the rope passes under your feet twice. You can also jump backwards or hop on one leg.

In **Double Dutch** two people turn two long ropes in opposite directions, and a third jumps in the middle. This takes a lot of practice and good timing. Skipping with tricks and competitions is called **rope skipping**. There are events for speed, for freestyle to music and for teams, and championships are held in Switzerland too.

Skipping needs strength in your legs, **endurance** and **coordination**. Your heart and circulation are trained, and you learn to move your arms and legs together in rhythm. That is why many athletes, for example boxers, use skipping for training. In the playground it is a popular game, often with rhymes that everyone says along.

gewusst: A skipping rope is one of the cheapest pieces of sports equipment and fits into any school bag.
Good rope skippers manage well over a hundred jumps in one minute.

teile.einleitung: Training theory explains how to train properly in order to become fitter, stronger or faster. It describes how much you should practise, when breaks are needed and how to plan a training session. Its principles apply to children in a gymnastics club just as much as to professionals.
wichtigste: Warming up prepares the muscles, heart and circulation for the effort.
After training and recovery the body reaches a higher level: supercompensation.
Rest days are important, because the body adapts during recovery.
In interval training effort and recovery alternate.
The load must increase step by step so that you keep making progress.
You measure your resting pulse in the morning straight after waking up.
The smallest training cycle is called a microcycle and usually lasts about a week.

abschnitte.text: Before every training session you should **warm up**. This prepares the muscles, heart and circulation for the effort. The muscles get a better blood supply and become warmer, so you are less likely to get injured. Typical activities are easy jogging, hopping and little games for about 10 to 15 minutes. At the end of training an easy cool-down jog helps the body to calm down.

Training is a stimulus that first tires the body. During recovery it does not just rebuild itself but goes beyond its old level. This model is called **supercompensation**. That is why **rest days** are so important, because the body becomes stronger during the break. If you train hard again too soon, performance drops; this is then called overtraining.

According to the principle of **progressive overload**, the load must be increased step by step so that further adaptations occur. In **interval training** periods of effort and recovery alternate regularly. Typical is the **rewarding break** (lohnende Pause), in which you recover only partly before the next interval. In strength training about 8 to 12 repetitions per set are regarded as a typical range for building muscle.

You measure your **resting pulse** in the morning straight after waking up, while still in bed. If it is higher than usual, you may be tired or ill. The maximum pulse is estimated with the rule of thumb 220 minus your age. For a 12-year-old this gives about 208 beats per minute. Heart rate watches help you train in the right zone.

A training year is divided into sections; this is called **periodisation**. The smallest cycle is the microcycle, which usually lasts about a week, followed by the meso- and macrocycle. A training plan helps you keep track. One example: anyone who runs for 40 minutes three times a week trains for 480 minutes in four weeks, that is 8 hours. The things trained are endurance, strength, speed, flexibility and coordination.

begriffe.erklaerung: Recovering beyond your old level of performance after training.
Training that alternates between effort and rest.
Heartbeats per minute at complete rest.
Dividing training into planned sections.
The smallest section of training, usually about a week.

gewusst: Muscles do not become stronger during training but in the recovery afterwards.
Children can learn coordination and skill especially well because their nervous system is still very adaptable.
Many professional athletes train for more than 20 hours a week.

teile.einleitung: The Bank for International Settlements, BIS for short, is an international organisation based in Basel. It is also called the “central banks’ bank”, because its customers are not private individuals but the national banks of many countries. It was founded in 1930 and is the oldest international financial organisation in the world.
wichtigste: The BIS has its headquarters in Basel, right next to the SBB railway station.
It was founded in 1930.
It is the oldest international financial organisation in the world.
Its members are central banks, including the Swiss National Bank.
Private individuals cannot open an account at the BIS.
It helps central banks to work together.
Important rules for banks are drawn up in Basel, for example “Basel III”.

abschnitte.text: The BIS is a bank for **central banks**, meaning the banks that issue the money in a country. In Switzerland that is the **Swiss National Bank**. The central banks invest part of their reserves with the BIS, for example. Their heads also meet regularly in Basel to exchange ideas.

The BIS was founded in **1930**, not long after the First World War. At first it was meant to help handle **reparations**, that is the payments Germany had to make after the war. Basel was chosen because Switzerland is neutral and easy to reach. Soon cooperation between central banks became its most important task.

The best-known building of the BIS is a round tower on Centralbahnplatz next to **Basel SBB station**. It was built in the 1970s. The BIS also has offices in Hong Kong and Mexico City. Special rights apply to its work, similar to those of embassies.

The **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** is based at the BIS. It draws up recommendations on how much capital of their own banks should have, so that they do not collapse in a crisis. These rules are named after the city: **“Basel I”, “Basel II” and “Basel III”**. Many countries all over the world adopt them into their laws.

The members of the BIS are over 60 central banks from all continents (as of 2026). Together they stand for most of the world economy. The BIS publishes statistics and studies about money, interest rates and financial markets. In this way it helps to keep the worldwide **financial system** stable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country’s bank that issues the money and keeps watch over interest rates.
Payments that a country has to make after a war to make up for damage.
A bank’s own money, which can absorb losses.
All the banks, stock exchanges and rules to do with money.

gewusst: Until 2003 the BIS kept its accounts in gold francs, an old unit of account based on gold.
Thanks to the BIS, the name “Basel” stands for banking rules all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Schwingen is a traditional Swiss form of wrestling and is regarded as the national sport. Two wrestlers fight in a round ring full of sawdust and hold on to each other's shorts.
wichtigste: Schwingen takes place in a round ring filled with sawdust.
The wrestlers wear short wrestling shorts made of tough twill (Zwilch).
A bout is won when the opponent lies with both shoulder blades in the sawdust.
The winner of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival is called the Schwingerkönig (wrestling king).
The Schwingerkönig traditionally receives a Muni, that is a bull.
Joel Wicki became Schwingerkönig in Pratteln in 2022.
After the bout the winner brushes the sawdust off the loser's back.

abschnitte.text: A fight is called a **bout** (Gang). It takes place in a round ring filled with **sawdust**. The sawdust cushions the falls. The wrestlers grip each other's shorts and try to bring the opponent to the ground with a **throw** (Schwung). There are many throws with their own names, for example the Kurz or the Hüfter.

Over their normal clothes the wrestlers wear short **wrestling shorts** made of **Zwilch**. Zwilch is a coarse, very tear-resistant fabric. Only this way can the shorts withstand the strong grips. A distinction is made between **Sennenschwinger** (herdsmen wrestlers), who usually wear dark trousers and a coloured shirt, and **Turnerschwinger** (gymnast wrestlers) in white clothing.

The winner is the one who puts the opponent into the sawdust so that **both shoulder blades** touch the ground at the same time. While doing so, the winner must still be holding the grip on the shorts with at least one hand. A **judge** assesses every bout. Points are awarded for good performances, and the best wrestlers receive a **wreath** of oak leaves.

The biggest festival is the **Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival**, which takes place every three years. The winner may call himself **Schwingerkönig**, the highest title in the sport. There are live prizes such as cattle or horses, and the king receives a **Muni** (bull). In 2019 Christian Stucki won in Zug, and in 2022 **Joel Wicki** from the Entlebuch won in Pratteln.

Respect is very important in Schwingen. After every bout the winner shakes hands with the loser and **brushes the sawdust off his back**. This shows that you stay fair despite a hard fight. Many wrestling festivals are also folk festivals with yodelling, the alphorn and flag throwing.

gewusst: A well-known historic wrestling festival is the Unspunnen Festival near Interlaken, which first took place in 1805.
Tens of thousands of people watch the Federal Festival in a huge arena.

teile.einleitung: A piece of sports equipment is an object you need to do a sport. It can be a ball, a racket, a board with wheels or a large piece of gymnastics apparatus. Many sports are even named after their equipment, for example skateboarding or curling.
wichtigste: Badminton is played with rackets and a shuttlecock.
A skateboard is a board with four small wheels.
The floorball ball is made of plastic and has holes.
For archery you need a bow and arrows.
In curling you slide a heavy stone across the ice.
Swiss wrestlers wear short wrestling shorts over their clothes.
You make a hula hoop circle around your hips.

abschnitte.text: Most ball sports have their own ball. The **floorball ball** is light, made of plastic and has many holes so that it does not fly too fast. In badminton you do not hit a ball but a **shuttlecock** made of feathers or plastic. Tennis, table tennis and squash are played with rackets or bats of different sizes.

A **skateboard** is a board with four small wheels that you ride standing up. It appeared in California in the 1950s and 1960s, when surfers also wanted to “surf” on land. Skateboarding has been an Olympic sport since 2021. Similar equipment includes inline skates, scooters and, in winter, snowboards.

In **curling** you slide a granite stone weighing almost 20 kilograms across the ice. Team-mates sweep with brooms in front of the stone so that it glides further or straighter. For ice hockey you need skates, a stick and a puck made of hard rubber. In bobsleigh, luge and skeleton you race down an ice channel.

In the gym there is large apparatus such as the horizontal bar, parallel bars, rings, balance beam and trampoline. Smaller equipment includes the skipping rope, ball, clubs and the **hula hoop**, which you make circle around your hips. Soft mats make sure that you land safely. Dumbbells in the gym are sports equipment too.

In **Schwingen** (Swiss wrestling) the competitors wear short **wrestling shorts** of tough fabric over their clothes so that they can hold on to their opponent. In stone throwing (Steinstossen) a large stone is thrown as far as possible; the Unspunnen stone is famous. In Hornussen you hit a small puck far across the field with a long, flexible stick. These sports exist almost only in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A light object with a ring of feathers used in badminton.
A flat disc of hard rubber used in ice hockey.
Short overtrousers of tough fabric for gripping in Swiss wrestling.
A piece of sports equipment used in archery to shoot arrows at a target.

gewusst: A shuttlecock can reach over 400 kilometres per hour in a hard smash.
Many curling stones are made of granite from a small Scottish island called Ailsa Craig.
The Unspunnen stone weighs over 80 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: The **Schwyzerörgeli** is a small accordion and the typical instrument of Swiss Ländler music. You hold it with both hands, pull and push the bellows and play on buttons. Its cheerful sound can be heard at many folk music festivals.
wichtigste: The Schwyzerörgeli belongs to the accordion family.
Instead of keys it has buttons.
The part that you pull apart and push together is called the bellows.
A button gives two different notes when you pull and when you push.
It is the most important instrument of many Ländler bands.

abschnitte.text: The Schwyzerörgeli belongs to the **accordion family**, like the piano accordion. In the middle are the **bellows**, a folded part that you pull apart and push together. This makes air flow through small metal tongues, the **reeds**, and makes them sound. On the right you play the melody with **buttons**, on the left the basses and accompanying chords.

What is special about the Schwyzerörgeli is that it is **bisonoric**. A button gives a different note when you pull the bellows than when you push them. So the player must know not only which button to press but also which way the bellows are moving at that moment. This takes practice, but it makes the instrument small and handy.

The Schwyzerörgeli appeared in the 19th century and quickly became popular, especially in Central Switzerland. Today it is the heart of many **Ländler bands**. Together with the clarinet, double bass or piano it plays Ländler, schottische, waltzes and polkas. Many children and young people learn it at music schools today.

gewusst: The name recalls the canton of Schwyz, where the instrument was built early on.

teile.einleitung: The assassination in Sarajevo was a murderous attack on 28 June 1914 on the heir to the Austrian throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and his wife Sophie. The fatal shots were fired by the young Gavrilo Princip. The assassination triggered the July Crisis, which led to the First World War a few weeks later.
wichtigste: The assassination took place on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie Chotek were killed.
The attacker was the 19-year-old Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip.
He belonged to a group of young men who were fighting against rule by Austria-Hungary.
The assassination triggered the July Crisis.
On 28 July 1914 Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
This turned into the First World War, which lasted until 1918.

abschnitte.text: **Franz Ferdinand** was the nephew of Emperor Franz Joseph and was due to become Emperor of Austria-Hungary. At that time Austria-Hungary was a large empire with many peoples and languages. Since 1908 **Bosnia and Herzegovina** had also belonged to it, which angered many Serbs. In June 1914 Franz Ferdinand visited military exercises in Bosnia and then travelled to Sarajevo.

In the morning the couple drove through Sarajevo in an open car. First a fellow conspirator threw a bomb, but it hit another vehicle. Later the driver took a wrong turning and stopped right next to **Gavrilo Princip**, near the Latin Bridge. Princip fired twice and fatally wounded Franz Ferdinand and Sophie.

Gavrilo Princip belonged to the group **Mlada Bosna**, which means “Young Bosnia”. The young men wanted the South Slavs no longer to be ruled by Austria-Hungary. They were supplied with weapons by a Serbian secret society. Princip was too young for the death penalty and was sentenced to 20 years in prison; he died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.

After the assassination, Austria-Hungary gave Serbia a harsh **ultimatum** with many demands. Serbia did not meet all of them, and on 28 July 1914 the war began. Because the great powers were linked by **alliances**, Russia, Germany, France and Great Britain soon entered the war. So within a few days a conflict in the Balkans became a world war.

About 17 million people died in the **First World War** by 1918. Afterwards Austria-Hungary fell apart, and new states such as Yugoslavia came into being. Switzerland stayed neutral but had to guard its borders with soldiers. Franz Ferdinand’s car and uniform can be seen today in the **Museum of Military History** in Vienna.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned murder, usually of an important person.
The person who is due to become the next king or emperor.
A final demand with a deadline, with the threat of force if it is not met.
The weeks in the summer of 1914 between the assassination and the start of the war.

gewusst: The attack succeeded only because the chauffeur had taken a wrong turning and had to stop.
28 June was also Franz Ferdinand and Sophie’s wedding anniversary.

teile.einleitung: Film technology includes all the equipment and methods used to record, edit and show films. These include cameras, lenses, lighting, picture formats and computer tricks. If you understand them, you see films with completely new eyes.
wichtigste: A cinema film is usually recorded and shown at 24 frames per second.
At 24 frames per second, a 90-minute film consists of 129 600 single pictures.
A wider aperture reduces the depth of field.
In chroma keying a single-coloured surface, usually green, is replaced by a different background.
The dolly zoom combines a camera move with a zoom in the opposite direction.
Motion capture transfers actors' movements to digital characters.
A UHD picture, often called “4K”, is 3840 pixels wide.

abschnitte.text: A film consists of many **single pictures** that are shown quickly one after the other. Because our eyes and brain no longer perceive them separately, we see smooth movement. Since the arrival of sound films, **24 frames per second** has been usual for cinema. A 90-minute film therefore consists of 90 times 60 times 24, that is 129 600 pictures. In the past they were exposed on **35 mm film**; today they are mostly recorded digitally.

The camera's **lens** focuses the light onto the film or the image sensor. The **aperture** is an adjustable opening that controls how much light comes in. The wider you open it, that is the smaller the f-number, the shallower the **depth of field**. Then only the person in the foreground is sharp and the background is blurred. According to the 180-degree rule, at 24 frames per second each frame is exposed for about 1/48 of a second so that movements look natural.

The camera can travel on a small trolley along rails; this trolley is called a **dolly**. Shots from above are made with a crane or a drone. In a **dolly zoom** the camera moves towards a person and zooms out at the same time, so that the background is eerily distorted. Alfred Hitchcock made this effect famous in 1958 in the film “Vertigo”. A **Steadicam** rig lets the camera glide smoothly while the operator walks.

The **aspect ratio** tells you how wide a picture is compared with its height. The wide cinema format **Scope** has a ratio of about 2.39 to 1, televisions usually 16 to 9. The resolution says how many pixels a picture is made of. A **UHD** picture, often called 4K, is 3840 pixels wide and 2160 pixels high. The more pixels, the finer the details you can see.

In **chroma keying** actors are filmed in front of a green or blue wall, which the computer later replaces with a different background. In **motion capture** actors wear suits with markers whose movements are recorded by cameras. This data is transferred to digital characters; this is how Gollum in “The Lord of the Rings” was created, for example. Computer animation creates whole worlds and mythical creatures. In the past, models, puppets and painted backgrounds were used instead.

Besides the picture, **sound** is very important: microphones record voices, and Foley artists recreate footsteps or creaking doors. In the cinema many loudspeakers all around provide **surround sound**. Today the film is usually shown with a **digital projector**, in the past with a film projector and large reels of film. In 3D films each eye sees a slightly different picture through glasses. This creates a three-dimensional impression.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of pictures per second, usually 24 in the cinema.
An adjustable opening in the lens that controls the amount of light.
The area in front of and behind the subject that appears sharp in the picture.
A method that replaces a single-coloured surface with a different picture.
Recording real movements that are transferred to digital characters.

gewusst: A cinema film on 35 mm film could be several kilometres long and weigh many kilograms.
Because of Hitchcock's film, the dolly zoom is also called the “Vertigo effect”.
Many television stations in Europe broadcast at 25 rather than 24 frames per second.

teile.einleitung: A legend is an old story that was passed on by word of mouth for a long time. Unlike a fairy tale, it is usually set in a real place, often with a true core. Many legends tell of devils, dragons, ghosts or brave heroes.
wichtigste: In the past legends were passed on by word of mouth from generation to generation.
Legends are usually connected with a particular place, person or event.
In the legend of the Devil's Bridge the people of Uri first sent a billy goat across the bridge.
The Pied Piper of Hamelin lures the rats out of the town with his pipe.
The Brothers Grimm collected not only fairy tales but also legends.
Many legends try to explain natural phenomena or strange places.

abschnitte.text: A **legend** is a traditional story tied to a particular place or time. In the past people told them to each other in the evening in the living room or while working. A legend often contains a true core that has been embellished with fantastic things. A **fairy tale**, on the other hand, usually begins with “Once upon a time” and takes place somewhere at some time. Legends feature devils, witches, giants, dwarfs or ghosts.

In the Schöllenen Gorge in the canton of Uri it was very difficult to build a bridge over the wild River Reuss. According to the legend, the **Devil** helped, but as payment he demanded the soul of the first one to cross the bridge. The clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across. In a rage the Devil wanted to destroy the bridge with a huge stone, but a pious woman scratched a cross into the stone and the Devil missed his target. This **Devil's Stone** lies near Göschenen today.

The town of Hamelin in Germany suffered from a plague of rats. A strange man lured the rats into the River Weser with his **pipe**. When the townspeople did not pay him, he came back and led 130 children out of the town, and they never returned. The legend gives the year 1284 as the date. What really happened is still unclear today; perhaps young people moved to new settlement areas in the east at that time.

Switzerland is rich in **Alpine legends**. According to legend, dragons are said to have lived on Mount Pilatus near Lucerne, and the ghost of Pontius Pilate is said to have haunted the mountain lake. The legend of the Sennentuntschi tells of herdsmen who made a doll out of rags that came to life. The story of **William Tell** is also regarded as a legend. In Valais people tell of the Gratzug and processions of the dead in the mountains.

In the 19th century people began to write legends down so that they would not be lost. The **Brothers Grimm** published their collection “German Legends” in 1816 and 1818. In Switzerland researchers such as Josef Müller collected legends from the canton of Uri. Legends show what people were afraid of in the past and how they explained the world to themselves. Today they live on in books, plays, films and as the names of places.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old, traditional story tied to a real place.
An invented story with no exact place or time.
Stories are told rather than written down.
A legend about the deeds of a brave hero.

gewusst: In 1977 the Devil's Stone near Göschenen was moved 127 metres because of the construction of the Gotthard motorway.
In Hamelin the legend of the Pied Piper is regularly performed as an open-air play in summer.
In the past it was sometimes forbidden to visit the mountain lake on Pilatus because people feared the ghost's anger.

teile.einleitung: A **rondo** is a piece of music in which a main section keeps coming back. In between, changing sections are heard that provide variety. The word comes from the French “rondeau”, which means something like a round song.
wichtigste: In a rondo the main section, the refrain, keeps coming back.
The changing sections in between are called couplets (episodes).
A typical pattern is A-B-A-C-A.
The final movement of a classical solo concerto is often a rondo.
Mozart's “Rondo alla turca” comes from the Piano Sonata in A major K. 331.

abschnitte.text: In a rondo the music begins with the main section **A**, the **refrain**. After that comes a different section, then A again, then a new section and so on. A typical pattern is **A-B-A-C-A**. The changing sections in between are called **couplets** or episodes. The refrain is usually in the home key, the couplets often in other keys.

abschnitte.titel: The rondo in the Classical period
abschnitte.text: In the Viennese Classical period the rondo was very popular, above all as the **final movement**. Many **solo concertos**, sonatas and symphonies by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven end with a cheerful, lively rondo. The returning refrain is easy to remember. Some rondos combine the form with sonata form; this is then called a **sonata rondo**.

One of the best-known rondos is the **“Rondo alla turca”** by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. It is the last movement of his **Piano Sonata in A major K. 331**. “Alla turca” means “in the Turkish style”. At that time the music of Turkish military bands with drums and cymbals was fashionable in Europe, and Mozart imitated their sound on the piano.

gewusst: Beethoven's well-known piano piece “Für Elise” is also built like a rondo, with an opening section that keeps coming back.

teile.einleitung: Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, inventor and businessman. He became very rich through the invention of dynamite. In his will he decided that his fortune should pay for the famous Nobel Prizes.
wichtigste: Alfred Nobel lived from 1833 to 1896.
He was born in Stockholm in Sweden.
In 1867 he invented dynamite, which made him rich.
He owned factories in many countries and registered over 350 patents.
In his will he founded the Nobel Prizes.
The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901.
The first Nobel Peace Prize went, among others, to the Swiss Henri Dunant.

abschnitte.text: Alfred Nobel was born in **Stockholm** on 21 October 1833. His father was an inventor who built sea mines in Russia. Alfred was taught privately and learnt to speak several languages fluently. He travelled a great deal, lived in Paris and founded companies all over Europe. He died on 10 December 1896 in San Remo in Italy.

The explosive **nitroglycerine** was very powerful but dangerous, because it could explode with just a jolt. In 1864 Nobel’s younger brother Emil was killed in an explosion at the family factory. Alfred looked for a safe solution. He mixed nitroglycerine with **kieselguhr**, a porous earth, and in 1867 received the patent for **dynamite**. Now the explosive could be transported safely and set off only with a detonator.

Dynamite changed the building of tunnels, roads and mines. A great deal of dynamite was used to build the **Gotthard railway tunnel** from 1872 to 1882. This let the workers make much faster progress than with gunpowder. Sadly, dynamite was also used as a weapon in war. With his factories in many countries, Nobel earned a huge fortune.

In 1888 Alfred’s brother Ludvig died, but a newspaper thought that Alfred had died. It called him a “merchant of death”. The story goes that Nobel was shocked by this and wanted to be remembered better. In his **will** of 1895 he decided that most of his fortune should pay for prizes. They were to go to people who had brought the greatest benefit to humankind.

The Nobel Prizes are awarded in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and for **peace**, and since 1969 also in economics. The ceremony takes place every year on 10 December, the day Nobel died. Most prizes are presented in Stockholm, but the Nobel Peace Prize is presented in **Oslo**. The first Nobel Peace Prize went in 1901 to **Henri Dunant** of Geneva, the founder of the Red Cross, and to the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. Many researchers from Switzerland have received a Nobel Prize since then.

begriffe.erklaerung: An explosive made of nitroglycerine and kieselguhr.
A very powerful but sensitive liquid explosive.
The right to be the only one to use an invention.
A written last wish saying what should happen to your property after your death.

gewusst: Alfred Nobel never married and had no children.
The chemical element nobelium is named after him.
As well as his work as a chemist, Nobel also wrote poems and a play.

teile.einleitung: An animated film is a film in which the movements are not simply filmed but created artificially, picture by picture. In the past every picture was drawn by hand; today many films are made on the computer. If the single pictures are shown quickly one after the other, our eyes believe that the characters are moving.
wichtigste: Animated films are made from many single pictures shown quickly one after the other.
“Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs” from 1937 was Disney's first feature-length cartoon.
“Toy Story” from 1995 was the first cinema film animated entirely on the computer.
In stop-motion, figures made of modelling clay or wood are moved and photographed picture by picture.
Hayao Miyazaki made “Spirited Away”.
The Swiss film “My Life as a Courgette” was nominated for an Oscar in 2017.
In 2002 “Shrek” became the first film to win the Oscar for best animated feature.

abschnitte.text: A film consists of many **single pictures**, usually 24 per second in the cinema. In an animated film each of these pictures is created artificially. If they are shown quickly one after the other, the eye can no longer see them separately. This creates the impression of smooth movement. You also know this effect from a flip book.

In a **cartoon** every picture is drawn and painted by hand. In 1928 “Steamboat Willie” came out, in which Mickey Mouse whistles at the wheel of a steamboat. In 1937 Walt Disney brought his first feature-length cartoon, “**Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs**”, to the cinema. The Japanese director **Hayao Miyazaki** of Studio Ghibli made “Spirited Away”, which won an Oscar in 2003.

In the **stop-motion** technique, figures made of modelling clay, wood or fabric are moved slightly and photographed picture by picture. This takes a great deal of work: one second of film needs many shots. The clay films “Wallace & Gromit” from England are well known; in them Gromit is a clever dog. The Swiss director Claude Barras made “My Life as a Courgette”, which was nominated for an Oscar in 2017.

In 1995 “**Toy Story**” by Pixar studio was the first feature-length cinema film animated entirely on the computer. In computer animation artists build characters as three-dimensional models and move them digitally. Today most big animated films are made this way, for example “Frozen” with the sisters Elsa and Anna. In 2002 “Shrek” became the first film to win the newly created Oscar for best animated feature.

Hundreds of people often work on an animated film for years. There are illustrators, animators, voice actors, musicians and programmers. First a **storyboard** is made, a kind of comic showing all the scenes. In Switzerland there is a degree course in animation at the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single picture in a film.
An animated film with figures that are moved and photographed picture by picture.
A drawn plan of all the scenes of a film.
Animation made from pictures drawn by hand.

gewusst: Hundreds of thousands of pictures were drawn for “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs”.
Many stop-motion films manage only a few seconds of finished film per working day.
Mickey Mouse made his first big appearance in “Steamboat Willie” in 1928.

teile.einleitung: The drum is one of the oldest musical instruments in the world. You strike a stretched skin, the drumhead, with sticks or your hands and so make a sound. Drums set the rhythm in music, from a rock concert to the Basel carnival.
wichtigste: A drum consists of a hollow body with a skin stretched over it.
It is played with drumsticks, beaters or bare hands.
Large drums tend to sound low, small drums tend to sound high.
Several drums and cymbals together are called a drum kit.
The big drum in the drum kit is called the bass drum and is played with the foot.
Well-known hand drums are the tambourine, the bongos and the djembe.
In Basel thousands of people drum and play the piccolo at carnival.

abschnitte.titel: How it is built and how it sounds
abschnitte.text: A drum has a round **shell** made of wood or metal. A **drumhead** is stretched over it, in the past made of animal skin, today often of plastic. When you strike the drumhead, it vibrates and makes the air in the shell sound. The tighter the drumhead is stretched, the higher the note. Large drums with a lot of air inside sound low, small drums bright.

In rock, pop and jazz bands a **drum kit** is played. It consists of several drums and cymbals that one person plays at the same time. The **bass drum** is struck with a foot pedal and gives the low basic beat. Then there are the snare drum, the tom-toms and cymbals such as the hi-hat. Drummers need their hands and feet at the same time for this.

Almost every culture in the world has drums. The **bongos** are two small drums joined together from Cuba, played with the fingers. The djembe comes from West Africa and is shaped like a goblet. The **tambourine** is a flat hand drum with small jingles around the edge that rattle when you shake it. In the orchestra there are the timpani, whose note can be tuned precisely.

The **Basel carnival** is the best-known drumming festival in Switzerland. It begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday at 4 o'clock in the morning with the **Morgestraich**, when all the lights in the dark city go out. Then groups called cliques march through the lanes with drums and piccolos. The Basel drum is a tall marching drum played with two wooden sticks. Many children learn drumming early on in the youth groups of the cliques.

Drums have existed for many thousands of years. In the past they were used not only for music but also for **sending signals** over long distances. Soldiers marched to the beat of drums, and in some parts of Africa messages were passed on with drums. To this day drums accompany festivals, dances and processions all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stretched skin on the drum that you strike.
The hollow body of the drum in which the sound is made.
Several drums and cymbals that one person plays together.
The regular sequence of beats that forms the pulse of the music.
The start of the Basel carnival at 4 o'clock in the morning.

gewusst: Drums belong to the percussion instruments; experts also call them membranophones.
Every year at the Basel carnival thousands of drummers are out and about for about three days.
The snare drum in the drum kit has wires stretched underneath that rattle when it is struck.

teile.einleitung: Winter sports are sports done on snow or ice. They include skiing, snowboarding, ice hockey, curling, bobsleigh and many more. With its Alps, Switzerland is one of the most important countries for winter sports.
wichtigste: In biathlon cross-country skiing and shooting are combined.
Nordic combined consists of ski jumping and cross-country skiing.
In skeleton you ride face down and head first through the ice channel.
The target circle in curling is called the house.
In ice hockey each team normally has six players on the ice.
The Lauberhorn race takes place in Wengen in the Bernese Oberland.
Skeleton is ridden on the Cresta Run in St Moritz.

abschnitte.text: In **alpine skiing** athletes race downhill, super-G, giant slalom and slalom. The **slalom** has the most gates and the shortest distances between them. The famous Lauberhorn race takes place in **Wengen** in the Bernese Oberland. Nordic skiing includes cross-country skiing and ski jumping, which together form Nordic combined. In **biathlon** cross-country skiing and shooting are combined.

In **bobsleigh** two or four people sit in a sled with steering. In luge you lie on your back, feet first. In **skeleton**, on the other hand, you ride face down and head first. On the **Cresta Run** in St Moritz a special form of skeleton has been ridden since the 19th century. The bobsleigh run from St Moritz to Celerina is the only natural ice run in the world.

**Ice hockey** is one of the most popular team sports in Switzerland. Each team normally has six players on the ice at the same time: five skaters and a goalkeeper. It is played with a hard puck that can fly very fast. In 2026 the men's Ice Hockey World Championship took place in Zurich and Fribourg.

In **curling** two teams slide heavy granite stones across the ice into a target circle, the **house**. The players sweep with brooms in front of the stone to influence its path. Switzerland regularly wins curling medals at world championships. Skating also includes figure skating and speed skating.

On a **snowboard** you stand sideways on a single wide board. There are races around gates and competitions in the halfpipe with jumps and spins. In freestyle skiing athletes show tricks on jumps and mogul slopes. These sports are younger and have been part of the Olympic Winter Games since the 1990s.

begriffe.erklaerung: A combination of cross-country skiing and shooting.
A competition made up of ski jumping and cross-country skiing.
A sledding sport ridden face down and head first.
The target circle in curling.

gewusst: St Moritz hosted the Olympic Winter Games twice, in 1928 and 1948.
The bobsleigh run in St Moritz is rebuilt from snow and water every winter.
The first Olympic Winter Games took place in Chamonix in France in 1924.

teile.einleitung: A rule of a game sets out what is allowed in a game and what is not. Without rules there would be constant arguments, and nobody would know who had won. Whether it is tag in the playground or a football match in the stadium, rules make a game fair and exciting.
wichtigste: The rules of a game make sure that everyone has the same chances.
The referee makes sure that everyone keeps to the rules.
With a whistle the referee stops the game.
If both teams have the same number of points at the end, it is called a draw.
In volleyball a team may touch the ball at most three times.
In handball you may take three steps with the ball in your hand.
In football a goal counts when the ball goes completely over the goal line.

abschnitte.text: Rules decide the aim of a game, the movements that are allowed and how you score points. They apply equally to everyone; this is called **fairness**. Anyone who breaks a rule commits a **foul** and is punished. Many sports have an international federation that sets the rules for the whole world.

The **referee** controls the game and makes sure that everyone keeps to the rules. With a **whistle** they stop the game, for example for a foul or a goal. In football they show the yellow card as a caution and the red card for a sending-off. Today video pictures often help with difficult decisions. The referee's decision stands, even if you do not agree.

In **football** a goal is scored when the ball goes completely over the goal line into the goal. In **volleyball** a team may touch the ball at most three times, and then it has to go over the net. In **handball** you may take three steps with the ball in your hand and hold it for at most three seconds. In floorball you may play the ball only with your stick, not with your hands.

Simple games have rules too. In **tag** one child has to catch the others, and whoever is caught is “it”. In hide-and-seek one child counts to a certain number while the others hide. The rules are often agreed together before the game. That is a good idea, because then there are fewer arguments.

At the end, whoever has more points or goals wins. If both teams have the same number, it is a **draw**. In some tournaments extra time or a penalty shootout is then needed. Being a good sport also means shaking hands with your opponent after the game.

begriffe.erklaerung: Behaving decently and honestly towards your opponent.
Breaking a rule, for example by pushing or holding.
Both sides have the same number of points at the end.
A penalty kick in football; Swiss German uses the word “Penalty”, while standard German says “Elfmeter”.

gewusst: The first standard football rules were written down in England in 1863.
Yellow and red cards have only existed in football since the 1970 World Cup.
The world football federation FIFA has its headquarters in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: A fable is a short story in which animals usually talk and act like humans. At the end there is often a lesson that shows how to behave wisely or rightly. Fables have been told for over 2500 years and can still be found in school books today.
wichtigste: A fable is a short story with animals that think and talk like humans.
At the end of a fable there is often a lesson, the moral.
The most famous writer of fables was Aesop from ancient Greece.
Each animal stands for a quality; the fox, for example, for cunning.
Well-known fables are “The Fox and the Crow”, “The Hare and the Tortoise” and “The Grasshopper and the Ant”.
In France Jean de La Fontaine became famous for his fables.
In the Middle Ages Ulrich Boner from Bern wrote an important German collection of fables.

abschnitte.text: A **fable** is a short, instructive story. The main characters are usually animals, sometimes also plants or objects, that talk and act like humans. The plot is simple and often has only two characters who compete against each other. At the end it becomes clear who acted wisely and who foolishly. This lesson is called the **moral**, and it is often the last sentence.

In fables each animal stands for a particular human quality. The **fox** is cunning, the lion powerful, the donkey stupid or stubborn, the lamb innocent. The ant is seen as hard-working, the wolf as greedy and dangerous. In this way fables can show human weaknesses without insulting anyone directly. Because everyone knows these roles, you understand the story straight away; this is called **typecasting**.

The most famous writer of fables was **Aesop**, who is said to have lived in ancient Greece in the 6th century BC. Little is known about his life; according to tradition he was a slave. Many fables that we know today go back to him. Later the Roman **Phaedrus** wrote fables in Latin. Over the centuries the stories were retold again and again.

In “The Fox and the Crow” the fox flatters the crow until it wants to sing and drops its **cheese**. In “The Hare and the Tortoise” the slow tortoise wins the race because the arrogant hare falls asleep on the way. In “The Grasshopper and the Ant” the hard-working **ant** gathers supplies in summer while the grasshopper only sings and goes hungry in winter. In “The Fox and the Grapes” the fox cannot reach the grapes and then claims they are sour anyway. That is where the expression “sour grapes” comes from (in German “Die Trauben sind ihm zu sauer”).

In the Middle Ages, around 1350, the Dominican monk **Ulrich Boner** from Bern wrote the collection of fables “Der Edelstein” (The Gemstone). It was printed in 1461 and is one of the first printed books in the German language. In the 17th century the Frenchman **Jean de La Fontaine** made the fable famous with elegant verses. In Germany Gotthold Ephraim **Lessing** wrote short fables in prose in the 18th century. To this day fables are retold in picture books and cartoons.

Fables are short and easy to understand, which is why they are often read in language lessons. Children learn to recognise a **lesson** in a story. You can write fables yourself by choosing two animals with opposite qualities. A fable usually has a clear structure with a starting situation, a conflict, a solution and a lesson. In this way pupils practise storytelling and thinking about how to behave rightly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short story, usually with talking animals and a lesson at the end.
The lesson you are meant to learn from a story.
Each character stands for a particular quality, such as the fox for cunning.
Text without rhymes and verses, that is ordinary language.

gewusst: The word fable comes from the Latin “fabula”, which means tale or story.
Many well-known sayings, such as the one about sour grapes, come from fables.
La Fontaine wrote about 240 fables in verse in total.

teile.einleitung: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world and winds over mountains and through deserts in northern China. For almost 2000 years it was built, extended and renewed again and again to protect the Chinese empire from attacks. Contrary to a widespread myth, it cannot be seen from the Moon.
wichtigste: The Great Wall of China is in northern China.
With all its sections it is over 21,000 kilometres long, according to a survey from 2012.
It was meant to protect China from attacks by horse-riding peoples from the north.
The first sections of wall were built over 2500 years ago.
Most of the parts visible today date from the Ming dynasty.
The wall cannot be seen from the Moon.
Since 1987 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage site.

abschnitte.text: The **Great Wall of China** is not really a single wall but a network of many walls, ramparts and ditches. It stretches from the Yellow Sea in the east to the Gobi Desert in the west. A survey by the Chinese authorities in 2012 found a good **21,000 kilometres** for all the sections together. That is more than half the distance round the Earth.

More than 2500 years ago, individual Chinese states were already building protective walls. From 221 BC the first emperor, **Qin Shi Huang**, had many of them joined up. Later dynasties continued building. The best-known parts with bricks and watchtowers were built during the **Ming dynasty** between 1368 and 1644.

The wall was meant to protect the empire from **horse-riding peoples** from the steppes in the north, such as the Xiongnu and later the Mongols. Soldiers stood on the watchtowers and passed on warnings with **smoke signals** and fires. In this way a message spread quickly over long distances. But the wall could not always stop attackers completely.

It is often claimed that the Great Wall of China is the only structure that can be seen from the Moon. That is a **myth**. The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away, and the wall is only a few metres wide. Even from a space station about 400 kilometres up it can hardly be made out with the naked eye, because it has similar colours to the landscape.

The wall has been a **UNESCO World Heritage** site since 1987 and is one of China’s most important sights. The well-restored sections at **Badaling** and Mutianyu near Beijing are especially well known. Millions of people visit the wall every year. However, many remote parts are crumbling because of wind, rain and people carrying stones away.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruling family that governs a country for a long time.
A tower from which soldiers watch the surrounding area.
A widespread story that is not true.
Especially valuable places that UNESCO wants to protect.

gewusst: In some places sticky rice is said to have been mixed into the mortar during building to make it stronger.
On public holidays the section at Badaling is so crowded that you can hardly move forward.

teile.einleitung: An age puzzle is a brain teaser in which you have to work out people’s ages from clues. One example: a father is four times as old as his son today, and in 20 years he will be twice as old. With a bit of logic or a simple equation you find out that the son is 10 years old today.
wichtigste: Age puzzles are word problems from mathematics.
The important thing is: everyone gets the same amount older each year.
The age difference between two people always stays the same.
You can solve such puzzles by trying things out or with an equation.
If the father is four times as old as the son today and twice as old in 20 years, the son is 10 today.
Age puzzles train logical thinking.

abschnitte.text: In an **age puzzle** you are given clues about people’s ages at different points in time. From these you have to work out their ages today. Typical phrases are “twice as old”, “five years ago” or “in ten years”. Puzzles like these are among the **word problems** in maths lessons. They are popular because you can solve them well in your head or on paper.

Everyone gets exactly one year older each year. That is why the **age difference** between two people always stays the same. If a mother is 30 years older than her daughter today, she will still be 30 years older in 50 years. The ratio of their ages, however, changes: a child of 2 and a mother of 32 means 16 times as old, but later only about twice as old. This insight helps with almost every age puzzle.

With simple puzzles you can **try things out systematically**. In the example, the father has to be four times as old as the son. If the son is 5, the father is 20; in 20 years they would be 25 and 40, which is not twice. If the son is 10, the father is 40, and in 20 years they are 30 and 60. Now the father is exactly twice as old, so the solution is right.

Older pupils solve such puzzles with an **equation**. You call the son’s age x; then the father is 4x years old. In 20 years: 4x + 20 = 2 times (x + 20). This becomes 4x + 20 = 2x + 40, so 2x = 20 and x = 10. At the end you should always check the solution with a **test**.

Age puzzles existed even in ancient times. A famous puzzle is about the Greek mathematician **Diophantus**, who probably lived in Alexandria in the 3rd century. His supposed gravestone is said to tell, in the form of a riddle, how long he was a child, a young man and married. Anyone who solves it gets an age of 84 years. Today you can find age puzzles in puzzle books, schoolbooks and quiz apps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A maths problem told in words.
A calculation with an equals sign and an unknown.
A letter such as x that stands for an unknown number.
A test of whether the solution you found really is right.

gewusst: The age difference between you and your parents stays exactly the same all your life.
When a child is 1 year old and the mother 31, the mother is 31 times as old, but this ratio gets smaller every year.
Puzzles about the age of Diophantus have been handed down for more than a thousand years.

teile.einleitung: The history of media tells how people have passed on news, knowledge and entertainment over time. It stretches from cave paintings and writing to printing, newspapers, radio and television, and on to the internet and streaming. Each new invention has greatly changed people's lives.
wichtigste: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable metal type in Mainz.
The Neue Zürcher Zeitung has been published since 1780.
The oldest surviving photograph was taken around 1826.
With Morse code, messages were telegraphed using short and long signals.
In 1876 the telephone made it possible to transmit the voice over wires.
Guglielmo Marconi is regarded as a pioneer of wireless radio transmission.
In 1989 the World Wide Web was invented at CERN in Geneva.
With streaming, content is played directly while it is being transmitted.

abschnitte.text: Over 30 000 years ago people were already painting animals on cave walls. Around 3200 BC the first **writing systems** appeared in Mesopotamia and Egypt. For a long time books were copied by hand, often by monks in monasteries such as St Gallen. Around 1450 **Johannes Gutenberg** in Mainz invented printing with movable metal type. Now books could be produced quickly and cheaply in large numbers.

Thanks to printing, printed news sheets soon appeared, and from the 17th century the first **newspapers**. The **Neue Zürcher Zeitung** has been published since 1780 and is one of the oldest newspapers in the world still being published. In the 19th century faster printing presses made newspapers affordable for many people. They reported on politics, business and events from all over the world. Today many people also read newspapers online.

Around 1826 the Frenchman **Joseph Nicéphore Niépce** took the oldest surviving photograph, a view from his window. At that time the exposure took many hours. From the 1840s the electric **telegraph** spread, sending messages over wires. It used **Morse code**, made of short and long signals and named after the American Samuel Morse. Soon cables even connected continents under the sea.

In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell patented the **telephone**, with which the human voice could be transmitted over wires. The Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** is regarded as a pioneer of wireless radio transmission, from which radio developed. In the 1920s regular radio broadcasts began in many countries, including Switzerland. In 1926 the Scot **John Logie Baird** demonstrated an early mechanical television picture in London. From the 1950s television found its way into more and more living rooms.

Music could first be stored on records, later on tapes and cassettes. In the 1980s the **compact disc**, CD for short, came onto the market, storing music digitally. At home people watched films on video cassettes and later on DVDs. With the MP3 format songs became small enough to send over the internet. Today most people listen to music via **streaming**, in which the content is played directly while it is being transmitted.

In 1989 the Briton **Tim Berners-Lee** invented the World Wide Web at the research centre **CERN** in Geneva. With it anyone could call up web pages with text, pictures and links. From the 2000s social networks and video platforms were added. Since about 2007, with the **smartphone**, people carry a telephone, camera, newspaper and television in one hand. Almost all earlier media are combined on the internet today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A means of passing on information, such as a book, radio or the internet.
A method of reproducing texts quickly with type.
A device that sends messages as electrical signals over wires.
A code of short and long signals for letters and numbers.
The network of linked web pages on the internet.

gewusst: The world's first website went online at CERN in 1991 and explained what the World Wide Web is.
The best-known Morse signal is SOS: three short, three long and three short signals.
Gutenberg's most famous work is a Bible, of which about 49 copies still survive today.

teile.einleitung: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth, bigger than any dinosaur. It can grow over 30 metres long and weigh as much as about 25 elephants. Even so, the giant feeds almost entirely on tiny crustaceans called krill.
wichtigste: The blue whale is the largest animal of all time.
It grows up to about 30 metres long and weighs well over 100 tonnes.
It is a mammal and breathes air.
It mainly eats krill, small crustaceans.
Instead of teeth it has baleen, with which it filters food out of the water.
Blue whales live in all the oceans.
Whaling almost wiped them out, and today they are protected.

abschnitte.text: The **blue whale** has a long, slim body with blue-grey skin dotted with lighter spots. It can grow over 30 metres long, about as long as three buses one behind the other. It often weighs well over 100 tonnes. Its **heart** alone weighs several hundred kilograms and is as big as a small car.

Although it is so huge, the blue whale eats almost nothing but **krill**, small crustaceans a few centimetres long. With its mouth open it takes in enormous amounts of water. Then it pushes the water out through its **baleen**, plates of horn in the upper jaw that work like a sieve. In one day a blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill.

Blue whales live in all the **oceans** of the world. In summer they feed in cold waters near the poles that are rich in food. In winter they migrate to warmer seas, where the young are born. They usually live alone or in small groups.

A blue whale calf is already about 7 metres long at birth. It drinks its mother’s very rich **milk** and at first puts on around 90 kilograms a day. Blue whales communicate with very deep, loud calls that can be heard hundreds of kilometres away. They are among the **loudest animals** in the world.

In the 20th century blue whales were hunted heavily with modern whaling ships, mainly for their blubber. Their numbers fell by more than 90 per cent. Since 1966 blue whales have been protected by the **International Whaling Commission**. Switzerland is a member of this commission and works to protect whales, even though it has no sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal whose young are fed with milk.
Small crustaceans that live in huge swarms in the sea.
Plates of horn in the mouth of some whales that act as a sieve.
Hunting whales, in the past mainly for blubber and meat.

gewusst: A blue whale’s tongue can weigh as much as an elephant.
Even though it is so big, a blue whale could not swallow a person, because its throat is quite narrow.

teile.einleitung: Tennis is a racket game in which two or four players hit a ball back and forth over a net with rackets. The aim is to hit the ball in such a way that the opponent can no longer return it within the rules. Thanks to stars such as Roger Federer and Martina Hingis, tennis is very popular in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In tennis you hit the ball with a racket.
Tennis balls are usually yellow.
A net is stretched across the middle of the court.
Every point begins with a serve.
After the first rally won, the score is 15.
Wimbledon in London is the most famous tournament and is played on grass.
Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slam tournaments, and Martina Hingis was number 1 at the age of 16.

abschnitte.text: Tennis is played as **singles** with two players or as doubles with four. A **net** is stretched across the middle of the court. Every point begins with a **serve**, after which the players hit the ball back and forth. The ball may bounce at most once on each side. The scoring is unusual: 15, 30, 40 and then game.

You need a **tennis racket** with tightly strung strings and a felt ball. The balls are usually yellow because that makes them easy to see on television and on court. In the past they were white. Tennis shoes have a special sole depending on the court surface.

The four most important tournaments are called the **Grand Slam**: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open. **Wimbledon** in London is the oldest; it has been played on grass since 1877. In Paris they play on red clay, in Melbourne and New York on hard courts. In Switzerland the Swiss Indoors in Basel and the tournament in Gstaad are well known.

**Roger Federer** from Basel won 20 Grand Slam tournaments, including Wimbledon eight times. He was world number 1 for many weeks and is regarded as one of the best players of all time. **Martina Hingis** became world number 1 in 1997 at the age of just 16. Stan Wawrinka won three Grand Slam titles, and Belinda Bencic became Olympic champion in 2021.

A forerunner of tennis is the French **jeu de paume**, in which the ball was at first hit with the hand. Modern lawn tennis developed in England in the 1870s. Tennis has been an Olympic sport again since 1988. Today millions of people all over the world play tennis, including in many Swiss clubs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first shot of a point, played from behind the baseline.
The four biggest and most important tennis tournaments.
A match between two teams of two players each.
A part of the match won by whoever first wins six games with a lead of two games.

gewusst: At Wimbledon the players have to be dressed almost entirely in white.
Roger Federer won the Swiss Indoors in his home town of Basel ten times.
A good serve can reach over 200 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: Muscles need energy to contract. This energy is supplied by a substance called ATP. The body has different ways of producing ATP, depending on how hard and for how long you exert yourself.
wichtigste: ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate and is the energy currency of the cells.
The ATP store in the muscle lasts only 2 to 3 seconds under maximum effort.
Without oxygen, glucose is broken down into lactate: anaerobic lactic.
Anaerobic glycolysis supplies a net total of only 2 ATP per glucose.
During long, steady efforts the body burns a lot of fat.
A marathon is run almost entirely aerobically.

abschnitte.text: **ATP** stands for **adenosine triphosphate**. It is the direct energy carrier for every muscle contraction. When ATP is split into **ADP** (adenosine diphosphate), energy is released. But the muscle stores only very little ATP: under maximum effort it lasts for about **2 to 3 seconds**. That is why ATP constantly has to be rebuilt from **creatine phosphate**, glucose or fat.

During short, very hard efforts **creatine phosphate** helps first. This pathway is called **anaerobic alactic** and lasts only a few seconds. After that, glucose is broken down without oxygen and **lactate** is produced. This pathway is called **anaerobic lactic**. It is fast but supplies a net total of only **2 ATP** per glucose molecule. Sprints over 100 to 400 metres are therefore strongly anaerobic.

With enough oxygen the body can break glucose down completely. Depending on how it is calculated, this gives about **30 to 38 ATP**, so much more.
