During steady endurance exercise it also burns a lot of **fat**. Fat reserves are very large, but they supply energy more slowly than carbohydrates. A **marathon** lasts over two hours and is run almost entirely **aerobically**.

At the start of an effort the need for oxygen rises faster than the heart and lungs can react. This gap is called the **oxygen deficit** and is covered anaerobically. After intense exercise the body goes on using more oxygen for a while; this is the **afterburn effect** (EPOC). The **respiratory quotient** (RQ) compares the carbon dioxide breathed out with the oxygen taken in. It is about 1.0 when only carbohydrates are burned and about 0.7 when only fat is burned.

gewusst: Every day a person builds up and breaks down roughly as much ATP as they weigh.
The power stations of the cells, in which ATP is produced with oxygen, are called mitochondria.

teile.einleitung: Everyday objects are things we use every day, often without thinking about them. They include the toothbrush, scissors, clock, umbrella, key and fridge. Behind each of these things lies an exciting invention with a long history.
wichtigste: You clean your teeth with a toothbrush.
You cut paper with scissors.
A clock shows the time.
An umbrella keeps us dry in the rain.
You unlock the front door with a key.
In the fridge, food stays cool and fresh.
Some well-known everyday objects were invented in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **toothbrush** has existed in a simple form for a very long time: in the past people chewed on twigs or used pig bristles. The first toothbrush with nylon bristles came on the market in the USA in 1938. Dentists recommend brushing twice a day for about two minutes. You should change your toothbrush about every three months. Electric toothbrushes are also very common today.

A pair of **scissors** consists of two blades that move around a pivot; it works like a double **lever**. Even the ancient Romans used scissors made of bronze and iron. For children there are craft scissors with rounded tips so that you do not hurt yourself. A Swiss classic is the **Swiss Army knife**, which has been supplied to the army since 1891. It contains a knife, scissors, a tin opener and much more.

A **clock** shows us the time; in the past with sundials and hourglasses, today with hands or digits. Switzerland is world famous for its watches, for example from the Jura, Geneva and Biel. The colourful plastic Swatch watch came on the market in 1983. With a **key** you open a lock, because its notches fit exactly with the pins in the lock. Today some doors can also be opened with cards, number codes or a mobile phone.

An **umbrella** has a frame of thin rods with waterproof fabric stretched over it. Umbrellas existed over 3000 years ago in China and Egypt, at first mainly for protection from the sun. Today there are pocket umbrellas that fold up small. A Swiss invention is the **Velcro fastener**, which the engineer Georges de Mestral invented after a walk with his dog. Burrs had stuck to the dog’s fur, and they gave him the idea.

In the **fridge** food stays fresh for longer, because bacteria multiply more slowly in the cold. A pump drives a refrigerant through pipes, which takes heat out of the air inside. The fridge gives off this heat again at the back, which is why it is warm there. About 5 degrees Celsius is recommended inside the fridge. In the past people cooled food with ice from lakes or stored it in a cool cellar.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thing you use in daily life.
A simple tool that lets you achieve a lot with little force.
A substance in the fridge that takes up heat and carries it away.
Something new that a person has thought up.

gewusst: The “Rex” vegetable peeler, found in many kitchens, was invented in Switzerland in 1947.
The idea for Velcro came from burdock, a plant with tiny hooks.
A fridge does not cool the kitchen if you leave the door open; it actually makes it warmer.

teile.einleitung: Famous athletes thrill millions of people with their achievements. Some set records that nobody beat for a long time; others made history outside sport too. Switzerland has also produced many world stars.
wichtigste: Jesse Owens won four Olympic gold medals in Berlin in 1936.
Pelé is the only footballer to have become world champion three times.
In 1976 Nadia Comăneci was the first to receive a score of 10.0 at the Olympic Games.
Michael Jordan won six NBA titles with the Chicago Bulls.
Muhammad Ali became world-famous as a boxer.
Serena Williams won 23 Grand Slam singles titles.
Rafael Nadal won the French Open 14 times.

abschnitte.text: The American **Jesse Owens** won four gold medals at the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin. Because he was black, his victories contradicted the racial ideology of the Nazis. In 2009 the Jamaican **Usain Bolt** ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, a world record that still stands today. He won eight Olympic gold medals in total.

The Brazilian **Pelé** became world champion in 1958, 1962 and 1970, which no other player has managed. In the 1990s **Michael Jordan** won six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. Many people regard him as the best basketball player of all time. Today footballers such as Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo are worldwide stars.

The Romanian **Nadia Comăneci** was only 14 years old when she received the first perfect 10.0 in gymnastics in Montreal in 1976. As a boxer, **Muhammad Ali** became Olympic champion and three times world heavyweight champion. He also stood up for the rights of black people in the USA. The swimmer Michael Phelps from the USA won 23 Olympic gold medals, more than anyone else.

**Serena Williams** from the USA won 23 Grand Slam singles titles and shaped women's tennis for two decades. The Spaniard **Rafael Nadal** won the French Open in Paris 14 times; on clay he was almost unbeatable. **Roger Federer** from Basel won 20 Grand Slam titles, 8 of them at Wimbledon. Martina Hingis was also world number one as a teenager.

Switzerland is particularly successful in skiing. **Vreni Schneider** from Glarus won three Olympic gold medals, and Bernhard Russi became Olympic downhill champion in 1972. More recently Lara Gut-Behrami and Marco Odermatt have had great successes in the World Cup. Nino Schurter became Olympic mountain bike champion in 2016, and Simon Ammann won Olympic gold in ski jumping four times.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who has won a gold medal at the Olympic Games.
The four most important tennis tournaments: the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and US Open.
The best performance ever measured in an event.
The winner of a world championship in a sport.

gewusst: Because the scoreboard in 1976 had only three digits, Nadia Comăneci's perfect 10.0 was at first shown as 1.00.
Muhammad Ali was originally called Cassius Clay.
During his world record Usain Bolt briefly reached a speed of over 40 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: The water safety check, WSC for short, tests whether a child can rescue themselves after falling into water unexpectedly. It consists of three tasks that are done one after the other without a break.
wichtigste: The water safety check has three tasks.
First you roll or tumble from the edge of the pool into deep water.
Then you stay afloat in one place for one minute.
Finally you swim 50 metres and climb out of the water.
There is no break between the tasks.
Anyone who passes receives a certificate.
Even after that, children only swim under supervision.

abschnitte.text: Many accidents in the water happen unexpectedly, for example when a child slips or falls off a jetty. The **water safety check** shows whether a child keeps their **bearings** in such a situation and can rescue themselves to the shore or the edge. It was developed in Switzerland by water safety experts and is regarded as an important basic skill.

In the first task you **roll or tumble** from the edge of the pool into deep water. Then you stay afloat in the same place for **one minute** without swimming away. Finally you swim **50 metres** and climb out of the pool **on your own**. Getting out is part of it too, because anyone who wants to save themselves has to get out of the water.

The three tasks follow **directly one after the other**. You may not hold on or rest in between. That makes it like a real **emergency**, in which you cannot take a break either. Anyone who manages all three tasks receives a **certificate**. Many children do the check in swimming lessons at **school**.

The check shows that a child can save themselves in the water. But it does not mean that they may swim alone. Children should **never** swim **without supervision**. Adults stay nearby and keep watching. In lakes and rivers there are also currents and cold water that can surprise even good swimmers.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are swimming safety rules, for example: only let children go to the water when accompanied and never jump into the water when overheated.
A child who passes the check can help themselves after falling into water, even without being able to do a particular swimming stroke perfectly.

teile.einleitung: Training principles are basic rules from training theory. They show how you should train so that the body adapts and your performance really improves.
wichtigste: Specificity: you mainly get better at what you train specifically.
Reversibility: what you no longer train, you lose again over time.
Only stimuli above the threshold trigger adaptations.
Individuality: a training plan must suit the person.
Variation: variety prevents standstill.
Continuity: only regular training brings lasting progress.
Periodisation divides the training year into phases.

abschnitte.text: Training only works if the stimulus is strong enough. This is described by the **stimulus threshold rule** (Arndt-Schulz rule): stimuli **below the threshold** have no effect, stimuli **above the threshold** trigger adaptations and stimuli that are too strong can do harm. The strength of a stimulus is called the **training intensity**, for example as weight, speed or heart rate. The **volume**, on the other hand, describes the total amount of training.

According to the **principle of specificity**, the body adapts to the type of load. Endurance training mainly improves endurance, strength training mainly strength. In English this is called the **SAID principle**. The **principle of individuality** requires that age, level of performance and capacity are taken into account, because people react differently to the same load.

Adaptations only happen if training stimuli are repeated **regularly**. This is the **principle of continuity**. Regularity is more important than single very hard sessions. If training is interrupted for a long time, the body loses strength or endurance again. This is described by the **principle of reversibility**.

If the stimuli stay the same for a long time, the body gets used to them and progress stalls. The **principle of variation** therefore recommends changing exercises, pace or methods again and again. It is just as important to **increase** the load slowly over time so that the stimulus stays above the threshold.

With **periodisation** the training year is divided into sections, for example the **preparation, competition and transition periods**. In preparation you lay the foundations, in competition you want to show your best form and in transition you recover actively. In this way your best performance should come exactly at the most important competition.

gewusst: Besides intensity and volume, the components of training load also include duration, density (that is the breaks) and frequency.
Recovery is part of training too, because the body only adapts during the break.

teile.einleitung: A building or structure is anything that people have built and that is firmly joined to the ground, from a house to bridges and huge dams. Some structures are world famous, such as the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt or the Great Wall of China. They tell us a lot about the people who built them.
wichtigste: Structures are buildings and installations made by people.
They include houses, towers, bridges, tunnels, walls and dams.
The Pyramids of Giza in Egypt are over 4500 years old.
The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world.
The Statue of Liberty in New York holds a torch up high.
There is a famous leaning tower in Pisa.
With the Gotthard Base Tunnel, Switzerland has the longest railway tunnel in the world.

abschnitte.text: A **structure** is something made by people that stands firmly on the ground. There is **building construction** such as houses and towers, and **civil engineering** such as roads, bridges and tunnels. Structures are planned by architects and civil engineers. They are built from materials such as stone, wood, concrete and steel.

abschnitte.titel: Famous structures of the ancient world
abschnitte.text: The **Pyramids of Giza** in Egypt were built about 4500 years ago as tombs for pharaohs. The biggest, the Pyramid of Khufu, was originally about 146 metres high. For almost 4000 years it was the tallest structure in the world. It is the only one of the seven wonders of the ancient world still standing today.

The **Great Wall of China** was meant to protect China from attacks from the north and stretches for thousands of kilometres. The **Statue of Liberty** in New York was a gift from France to the USA and was unveiled in 1886. The **Leaning Tower of Pisa** in Italy is the bell tower of the cathedral and began to lean even while it was being built, because the ground is soft. Millions of people visit landmarks like these every year.

At 57 kilometres, the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is the longest railway tunnel in the world; it opened in 2016. At 285 metres, the **Grande Dixence** dam in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world. The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe. Castles, monasteries and cathedrals such as Bern Minster are also among the country’s well-known buildings.

Especially valuable buildings are **listed** and protected as monuments. UNESCO keeps a list of **World Heritage** sites, which includes, for example, the Pyramids, the Great Wall of China and the Old City of Bern. Such structures are to be preserved for future generations. Today builders also pay attention to saving energy and using environmentally friendly materials.

begriffe.erklaerung: Building above the ground, for example houses and towers.
Building roads, bridges, tunnels and pipelines.
A specialist who calculates that a structure will stand firmly.
Rules that protect valuable old buildings from being destroyed.

gewusst: The Leaning Tower of Pisa was made safe in the 1990s so that it would not fall over.
About 28 million tonnes of rock were dug out to build the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
The Statue of Liberty is hollow inside and has an iron framework designed by Gustave Eiffel.

teile.einleitung: William Tell is the best-known hero of Switzerland. According to the legend, he had to shoot an apple off his son's head with his crossbow because he had not saluted the hat of the bailiff Gessler. Whether Tell really existed is uncertain, but his story has been told for over 500 years.
wichtigste: William Tell is a hero from the founding legend of Switzerland.
According to the legend, he came from Bürglen in the canton of Uri.
In Altdorf people were supposed to salute a hat on a pole.
Tell shot an apple off his son's head with his crossbow.
Later he killed the bailiff Gessler in the Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht.
In 1804 Friedrich Schiller made the story world-famous with his play.
Historians doubt that Tell really lived.

abschnitte.text: The legend is set around the year 1300, when the Habsburgs ruled Central Switzerland. The **bailiff Gessler** had a hat placed on a pole in Altdorf, and everyone had to salute it. William Tell walked past with his son Walter without saluting the hat. As a punishment he had to shoot an apple off his son's head with his **crossbow**. The shot succeeded, but Tell had a second arrow ready, which was meant for Gessler.

Gessler had Tell taken in chains onto a boat to lock him up. On Lake Uri a violent storm blew up, and Tell was untied so that he could steer. He leapt ashore onto a flat rock and escaped; this place is called the **Tellsplatte** today. In the **Hohle Gasse** (the sunken lane) near Küssnacht he lay in wait for Gessler and killed him with an arrow. In the legend this deed stands as a sign of the Swiss Confederates' struggle for freedom.

The oldest written version is in the **White Book of Sarnen**, which was written around 1470. That is about 150 years after the supposed deed. There are no documents from that time that mention Tell or Gessler. The Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus already told a very similar story about an apple shot by a hero called Toko. That is why most historians regard Tell as a **legendary figure**.

In 1804 the German poet **Friedrich Schiller** wrote the play “William Tell”, which made the story known worldwide. In 1829 the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini wrote an opera whose overture is still very famous today. In Altdorf and Interlaken there are **Tell Plays**, at which the play is performed. The Tell Monument in Altdorf by Richard Kissling was unveiled in 1895. It shows Tell with his crossbow, holding his son by the hand.

William Tell stands for **freedom** and resistance against unjust rulers. He became a symbol of Switzerland that can be found on stamps, posters and products. For example, since 1931 the crossbow has been part of a Swiss mark of origin for goods. In Bürglen there is a Tell Museum, and on Lake Uri stands **Tell's Chapel**. Even though he probably never lived, almost every child in Switzerland knows his story.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old story that may have a true core.
A weapon with a bow that shoots bolts.
An official who governed an area on behalf of a ruler.
Allied valley communities from which Switzerland grew.

gewusst: The overture to Rossini's opera “William Tell” is still often heard in films and adverts today.
The Tell Plays in Interlaken have been performed in the open air since 1912.
In the legend Tell hit the apple on his first attempt without hurting his son.

teile.einleitung: The waltz is a couple dance in three-four time in which you turn in a circle. It became especially popular in Vienna in the 19th century. To this day it is part of every ball.
wichtigste: The waltz is in three-four time: one, two, three.
Johann Strauss (the son) was called the “Waltz King”.
His best-known waltz is “The Blue Danube” from 1867.
The Viennese waltz is much faster than the slow waltz.
The slow waltz is also called the English waltz.

abschnitte.text: The waltz is in **three-four time**, so you always count “one, two, three”. The couples turn in circles across the dance floor. The word comes from the German “walzen”, meaning “to turn”. The waltz developed from older turning dances such as the **Ländler**. At first some people thought it improper that the couples held each other so closely.

**Johann Strauss (the son)** lived in **Vienna** in the 19th century. He composed a great many waltzes and led his own orchestra. This made him world-famous, and he was given the nickname **“Waltz King”**. His father Johann Strauss was already a well-known waltz composer. His brothers Josef and Eduard Strauss also wrote dance music.

The best-known waltz is called **“The Blue Danube”** and was written in **1867**. In German it is known for short as the **Donauwalzer** (Danube Waltz). It is regarded as Austria's unofficial anthem. Every year it is played at the **New Year's Concert** of the Vienna Philharmonic, which is shown on television in many countries. You often hear it on Swiss radio on New Year's Day too.

In dancing there are two kinds. The **Viennese waltz** is danced at about 60 bars per minute, and the couples turn very quickly. The **slow waltz** has only about 30 bars per minute and feels calm and floating. It developed in England and is therefore also called the **English waltz**. Both are among the standard dances taught in dance schools.

gewusst: Every year Vienna has a great many balls where the waltz is danced; the most famous is held in the State Opera.
Composers such as Frédéric Chopin and Pyotr Tchaikovsky also wrote waltzes.

teile.einleitung: Digital entertainment is everything we use to pass the time on screens and the internet: streaming films and series, listening to music, watching videos and playing games. For many children and teenagers in Switzerland it is a regular part of everyday life. But to make it fun, you also need to know about costs, data and risks.
wichtigste: With streaming, data is transferred during playback and not stored permanently.
A two-hour film at 5 megabits per second needs about 4.5 gigabytes of data.
In Switzerland and Europe the PEGI rating shows from what age a game is suitable.
Free-to-play games cost nothing but make money from purchases in the game.
In 2018 Belgium classified paid loot boxes as gambling.
Deepfakes are videos faked with artificial intelligence that look deceptively real.
The JAMES study by the ZHAW regularly examines how young people in Switzerland use media.

abschnitte.text: With **streaming**, a film or a song is transferred bit by bit while it plays and is not stored permanently afterwards. With a **download**, the whole file is first loaded onto the device and stays there. Streaming therefore needs a stable internet connection. A film that runs for two hours at 5 megabits per second uses about 4.5 gigabytes of data. On your mobile phone when you are out and about, this can quickly use up your data plan.

Today many people listen to music through streaming services such as Spotify and watch videos on platforms such as **YouTube**. Series and films are available from providers such as Netflix or Disney+ for a monthly fee; this is called a **subscription**. When you watch many episodes of a series in one go, it is called **binge-watching**. Because the next episode often starts automatically, you hardly notice how time passes. Podcasts, that is programmes to listen to, are also very popular.

Video games are played on consoles, computers or smartphones. Some people try to finish a game as fast as possible in a **speedrun** and compare their times. In **e-sports** professionals compete against each other in tournaments, and thousands watch online. On platforms such as Twitch players broadcast their games live. Gaming together with friends can be great fun, including over the internet.

Many games are **free-to-play**, so they cost nothing, but they make their money from purchases in the game, for example for costumes or extras. With **loot boxes** you pay for a surprise box without knowing what is inside. Because this is reminiscent of gambling, Belgium classified paid loot boxes as gambling in 2018, which effectively banned them. It is a good idea to agree a spending limit with your parents. Subscriptions to streaming services also cost money every month.

abschnitte.titel: Protecting young people and staying safe
abschnitte.text: The **PEGI** rating uses numbers such as 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18 to show from what age a game is suitable. In 2022 Switzerland passed a law on protecting minors with regard to films and video games, which requires age checks when they are sold. With artificial intelligence it is now possible to make **deepfakes**, that is deceptively real videos with swapped faces or voices. That is why you should not believe everything you see online. Never give personal data or passwords to strangers.

Since 2010 the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW) has used the **JAMES study** every two years to examine how young people in Switzerland use media. Almost all teenagers have their own smartphone. Their favourite activities include listening to music, watching videos and using social networks. Experts recommend making sure you get enough breaks, sleep and exercise. A good mix of screen time and experiences outdoors is good for body and mind.

begriffe.erklaerung: Content is played directly while it is being transferred.
A measure of how much data flows through the internet per second.
A virtual surprise box in a game whose contents are random.
A very real-looking video faked with artificial intelligence.
Watching many episodes of a series one straight after the other.

gewusst: JAMES stands for the German words for youth, activities, media, survey Switzerland (Jugend, Aktivitäten, Medien, Erhebung Schweiz).
One gigabyte equals 8000 megabits, which is why a two-hour film at 5 megabits per second needs about 4.5 gigabytes.
The biggest e-sports tournaments fill entire stadiums with spectators.

teile.einleitung: The Bretton Woods system was an order for the world’s money that applied after the Second World War. It was agreed in July 1944 at a conference in the town of Bretton Woods in the USA, where the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were also founded. The countries’ currencies were firmly tied to the US dollar, and the dollar to gold.
wichtigste: The Bretton Woods conference took place in the USA in July 1944.
Representatives of 44 states took part.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were agreed there.
The currencies had fixed exchange rates to the US dollar.
Dollars could be exchanged for gold at the US central bank at 35 dollars an ounce.
In 1971 the USA ended the dollar’s link to gold.
In 1973 the system finally collapsed.

abschnitte.text: In July 1944, while the Second World War was still going on, experts from **44 states** met at the Mount Washington Hotel in **Bretton Woods** in the US state of New Hampshire. They wanted to stop the economic crises of the 1930s from happening again. At that time countries had devalued their currencies against each other and put up trade barriers. Key figures were the Briton **John Maynard Keynes** and the American Harry Dexter White.

Every currency had a fixed **exchange rate** to the US dollar, which was allowed to move only a little. The dollar itself was tied to gold: other central banks could exchange 35 dollars for one ounce of gold. This made the dollar the world’s most important **reserve currency**. The Swiss franc also had a fixed rate to the dollar at the time, about 4.30 francs for 1 dollar.

Two important organisations were agreed at the conference. The **International Monetary Fund**, IMF for short, helps countries with payment problems and keeps watch over currencies. The **World Bank** first gave loans for rebuilding Europe and today mainly supports poorer countries. Both have their headquarters in Washington.

In the 1960s the USA spent more and more money, among other things on the Vietnam War. There were far more dollars than there was gold. In August 1971 President **Richard Nixon** announced that dollars would no longer be exchanged for gold. In 1973 most countries gave up fixed rates, and since then there have been **floating exchange rates**.

Switzerland did not take part in the conference in 1944 and for a long time did not join the IMF or the World Bank. Only after a **popular vote** in May 1992 did it become a member of both organisations. Today Switzerland leads its own voting group of several countries in the IMF. After the end of Bretton Woods, the franc became much stronger against the dollar.

begriffe.erklaerung: The price of one currency in another currency.
A currency that many other countries use as their reference.
A unit of weight for gold, about 31 grams.
An organisation that helps countries with money problems.

gewusst: Under Bretton Woods a dollar cost over 4 francs; today it is usually worth less than 1 franc (as of 2026).
The Mount Washington Hotel, where the conference took place, is still a hotel today.

teile.einleitung: A cinema film is a feature film that is first shown on the big screen in the cinema. Films such as “Star Wars”, “Jurassic Park” or “The Lion King” became worldwide successes that thrilled millions of people. Going to the cinema has been a shared experience for more than a hundred years.
wichtigste: Cinema films are first shown in the cinema on a big screen.
A feature film usually lasts about one and a half to two and a half hours.
“Avatar” is (as of 2026) the highest-grossing cinema film of all time worldwide.
George Lucas invented “Star Wars” and directed the first film in 1977.
In 1993 Steven Spielberg made the dinosaur film “Jurassic Park”.
In “The Lion King” Simba is meant to succeed his father Mufasa on the throne.
The film character Indiana Jones is an archaeologist.

abschnitte.text: A **cinema film** is a film made to be shown in the cinema. It is usually a **feature film** with an invented story, performed by actors or as animation. In the cinema it is dark, the screen is huge and the sound comes from many loudspeakers. After a few weeks or months most films also come out on streaming services or on television. Before the film there are often adverts and **trailers** for other films.

**Steven Spielberg** is one of the most successful directors of all time. In 1993 he made “**Jurassic Park**”, in which scientists bring dinosaurs back to life. In the film the genetic material comes from mosquitoes that had sucked dinosaur blood and were trapped in **amber**. Thanks to computer tricks the dinosaurs looked more real than ever before. Spielberg also made “E.T.” and, from an idea by George Lucas, the films about the archaeologist **Indiana Jones**.

**George Lucas** invented the film series “**Star Wars**” and directed the first film in 1977. In it rebels fight against an evil empire, and the Jedi Knights use the mysterious Force. In the second film from 1980 Luke Skywalker learns that **Darth Vader** is his father. This scene is one of the most famous surprises in film history. Today Star Wars belongs to the Disney group, and there are many films and series.

Disney's “**The Lion King**” came out in 1994 and tells of the lion cub **Simba**, who is meant to succeed his father Mufasa on the throne. His wicked uncle Scar wants to take the throne from him. The film was a huge success, its songs are known all over the world, and in 2019 a computer-animated remake came to the cinema. An older classic is “**The Wizard of Oz**” from 1939, in which Dorothy and her little dog Toto reach a magic land. It was one of the first big colour films.

In “**Back to the Future**” from 1985 the inventor Doc Brown turns a sports car, a DeLorean, into a time machine. The teenager Marty McFly travels into the past with it. The highest-grossing cinema film worldwide is (as of 2026) “**Avatar**” by James Cameron from 2009. It is set on the moon Pandora and was shown in 3D. The success of a film is measured by its **box-office takings**, that is the money from cinema tickets.

In Switzerland there are cinemas in almost every town, from large **multiplex cinemas** with many screens to small arthouse cinemas. Films are often shown in several versions: in German, French, Italian or in the original language with subtitles. In summer **open-air cinemas** are very popular, for example on Lake Zurich or on the Piazza Grande in Locarno. Swiss films such as “Heidi” also draw many people to the cinema. In Switzerland a cinema ticket usually costs between about 15 and 25 francs (as of 2026).

begriffe.erklaerung: A film with an invented story, usually more than an hour long.
The large pale surface onto which the film is projected in the cinema.
The person who leads the filming.
The money a film earns from cinema tickets sold.
Another film that continues the story of an earlier film.

gewusst: “Avatar” earned over two billion dollars worldwide.
For the time machine in “Back to the Future” to work, the car had to reach a speed of 88 miles per hour.
In German-speaking countries the first “Star Wars” film was at first simply called “Krieg der Sterne” (War of the Stars).

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has produced many important **composers**. Some became known for songs and choral music, others for operas, orchestral works or new ideas for music teaching. Some worked mainly abroad.
wichtigste: Émile Jaques-Dalcroze developed eurhythmics in Geneva, a way of teaching music through movement.
Hans Georg Nägeli from Zurich is regarded as the “father of singing” of Switzerland.
Frank Martin was born in Geneva in 1890.
Othmar Schoeck is known especially for his art songs.
Heinz Holliger is world-famous as an oboist.
Joachim Raff was born in 1822 in Lachen in the canton of Schwyz.
As general manager, Rolf Liebermann ran the opera houses in Hamburg and Paris.

abschnitte.text: **Hans Georg Nägeli** from Zurich was a music teacher, composer and publisher. He promoted singing in choirs and schools so strongly that he is called the **“father of singing”** of Switzerland. **Émile Jaques-Dalcroze** worked in **Geneva** and developed **eurhythmics**, in which you learn music through movement. Both shaped music teaching far beyond Switzerland.

**Frank Martin** was born in **Geneva** in 1890 and wrote orchestral works, concertos and oratorios. **Ernest Bloch** also came from Geneva. He emigrated to the USA, where among other things he wrote **“Schelomo”** for cello and orchestra. The work is named after the biblical King Solomon. **Arthur Honegger** had Swiss parents and became famous with the orchestral piece “Pacific 231”, which portrays a steam locomotive.

**Othmar Schoeck** is known above all for his **art songs**, that is poems skilfully set to music for voice and piano or orchestra. He wrote hundreds of such songs. **Joachim Raff** was born in 1822 in **Lachen** in the canton of Schwyz. He worked for some years as Franz Liszt's assistant in Weimar and wrote many symphonies.

**Rolf Liebermann** from Zurich was a composer and above all a well-known **general manager**, that is the head of an opera house. He ran the State Opera in **Hamburg** and the Opera in **Paris**. **Heinz Holliger** is known as a world-class **oboist** and is also a composer and conductor. He often writes modern music with unusual sounds.

Almost everyone in Switzerland knows one work: the **Swiss Psalm**. Its melody was written by the monk **Alberich Zwyssig** in 1841. Since 1981 it has officially been the national anthem of Switzerland. In this way a simple choral song by a Swiss composer became the best-known piece of music in the country.

gewusst: Ernest Bloch taught many young composers in the USA.
Heinz Holliger extended the playing technique of the oboe, for example with multiphonics, in which the instrument produces several notes at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Pitch tells you how high or low a note sounds. It depends on how fast something vibrates: fast vibrations sound high, slow ones low. That is why a bird whistles high and a bear growls low.
wichtigste: Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates.
The faster the vibration, the higher the note.
A short, thin string sounds higher than a long, thick string.
The double bass sounds lower than the violin.
Grown men usually have deeper voices than women and children.
High notes are written higher up on the staff.
A metal tuning fork always produces exactly one note.

abschnitte.text: Every note is produced by a **vibration**, which spreads through the air as a sound wave. How many times something swings back and forth per second is called its **frequency**, measured in hertz (Hz). The concert pitch a¹, to which orchestras tune, vibrates 440 times per second. If the frequency doubles, the note sounds exactly one octave higher. People hear notes between about 20 and 20000 Hz; with age the upper limit gets lower.

On string instruments the length, thickness and tension of the string determine the pitch. A **short, thin** and tightly stretched string sounds high, a long, thick one sounds low. That is why the small violin is high and the big double bass is low. With wind instruments something similar applies to the column of air: a piccolo sounds high, a tuba low. With glasses of water, the more water you pour in, the lower the sound when you tap them.

Our voice is produced by the **vocal folds** in the larynx, which vibrate when we speak and sing. Children and women usually have shorter vocal folds and therefore higher voices. In boys the larynx and vocal folds grow during puberty and the voice gets deeper; this is called the **voice breaking**. In a choir, from high to low, there are soprano, alto, tenor and bass.

In musical notation high notes are written higher up on the staff and low notes lower down. The notes have names such as c, d, e, f, g, a and b. So that all instruments fit together, they are tuned to a reference note, for example with a **tuning fork** or an electronic tuner. Very few people have **perfect pitch** and can recognise a note without help.

There are sounds that are too high or too low for humans. Sounds above about 20000 Hz are called **ultrasound**; bats use it to find their way in the dark. Dogs also hear much higher sounds than we do, which is why there are dog whistles that we can hardly hear. Very low sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound; elephants use it to communicate over long distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The unit for vibrations per second, abbreviated Hz.
A metal fork that produces exactly one note when struck.
The voice getting deeper during puberty.
Sounds that are too high for the human ear.

gewusst: When an ambulance drives past you, its siren suddenly sounds lower; this is called the Doppler effect.
The lowest note on a piano has only 27.5 vibrations per second.
The tuning fork was invented in 1711 by the English trumpeter John Shore.

teile.einleitung: A screenplay is the written plan for a film or a series. It contains all the scenes, places, actions and dialogue, so that the whole film crew knows what is to be shot. Good screenplays often follow proven rules of storytelling.
wichtigste: A screenplay describes the scenes, plot and dialogue of a film.
One page in the standard format equals about one minute of screen time.
The classic three-act structure divides a story into set-up, confrontation and resolution.
Before the screenplay, a logline and a treatment are often written.
The “hero's journey” goes back to the mythologist Joseph Campbell.
In 1979, with his book “Screenplay”, Syd Field shaped the model with two plot points.
Storytelling principles such as Chekhov's gun help to make a story hang together.

abschnitte.text: A **screenplay** is the written basis for a film. Each scene begins with a heading that says whether it takes place inside or outside, where and at what time of day. This is followed by a short description of the action and the characters' **dialogue**. The screenplay is written in a special format, often in the Courier font. Because one page equals about **one minute** of film, a feature film usually has around 90 to 120 pages.

abschnitte.titel: From the idea to the script
abschnitte.text: It starts with an idea, which is summed up in one or two sentences in a **logline**. After that a short outline of the story is often written. In the **treatment** the plot is told scene by scene in prose, but still without finished dialogue. Only then is the actual screenplay written, and it is often revised several times. Some screenplays are written over many years and in many versions.

Many films follow the **three-act structure**. In the first act, the set-up, you get to know the characters and their world. In the second act, the confrontation, the main character runs into problems and opponents. In the third act comes the climax and the **resolution**. In 1979 the screenwriting teacher **Syd Field** described in his book “Screenplay” two turning points, called plot points, which lead from one act to the next.

The American mythologist **Joseph Campbell** studied legends and fairy tales from all over the world. He discovered that many hero stories follow a similar pattern, the **hero's journey**. The heroine or hero leaves the familiar world, passes tests, finds helpers and returns changed. Hollywood often uses this model, for example in “Star Wars” or “The Lion King”. This makes stories feel familiar and exciting at the same time.

A **MacGuffin** is an object that everyone is chasing but which is itself unimportant; the director Alfred Hitchcock made the term well known. According to **Chekhov's gun**, a gun hanging on the wall in the first act must be fired later. This means that nothing should appear in a story without a reason. A **deus ex machina** is a sudden rescue from outside that has hardly been prepared. In ancient Greek theatre a god floated onto the stage with a crane for this; today the trick is regarded as a rather weak solution.

People who write screenplays work closely with the director and the producers. Some screenplays are **original stories**, others are adaptations of novels or plays. That is why the Oscars have two awards, one for the best original screenplay and one for the best adapted screenplay. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Culture and other bodies support the development of screenplays with **film funding**. You can learn screenwriting at film schools, for example in Zurich or Lausanne.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea of a film summed up in one or two sentences.
A preliminary stage of the screenplay that tells the plot scene by scene without finished dialogue.
A turning point that steers the story in a new direction.
An object that drives the plot but is itself unimportant.
Latin for “god from the machine”, a sudden rescue from outside.

gewusst: Because one page of a screenplay equals about one minute of film, the length of a film can be estimated well before shooting.
The term deus ex machina comes from ancient theatre, where gods were lifted onto the stage with a crane.
Joseph Campbell described the hero's journey in 1949 in his book “The Hero with a Thousand Faces”.

teile.einleitung: Absolute zero is the lowest temperature there can possibly be. It is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, or 0 kelvin. It cannot get any colder, and this point can never be reached completely.
wichtigste: Absolute zero is -273.15 °C.
On the kelvin scale it is exactly 0 kelvin.
At this temperature the particles would have the lowest possible energy of motion.
You can only get closer and closer to absolute zero but never reach it completely.
The kelvin scale is named after the British physicist Lord Kelvin.
Very low temperatures are needed for superconductors and particle accelerators.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of tiny particles that are constantly moving and jiggling. **Temperature** shows how strongly they move: the warmer, the faster. If you cool a substance, its particles get slower and slower. At **absolute zero** they would have the lowest possible energy. This point is at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.

Scientists often measure temperatures in **kelvin**. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, that is at 0 kelvin, and has no negative numbers. A step of one kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius. So water freezes at about 273 kelvin and boils at about 373 kelvin. The British physicist William Thomson, later **Lord Kelvin**, proposed this scale in 1848.

A basic law of physics, the **third law of thermodynamics**, says that absolute zero can never be reached completely. But researchers have already come within tiny fractions of a kelvin of it. To do this they use lasers, magnetic fields and very cold liquids. Liquid **helium** boils at about 4.2 kelvin and is an important coolant. At extremely low temperatures strange states arise, such as the Bose-Einstein condensate.

Some metals conduct electricity with no resistance at all at very low temperatures; they are called **superconductors**. The Dutchman Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered this in 1911 with mercury. Superconducting magnets are found in MRI scanners in hospitals, which can be used to look inside the body. Quantum computers are also cooled almost to absolute zero. That is how their sensitive components work.

abschnitte.titel: Cold at CERN and in space
abschnitte.text: At the research centre **CERN** near Geneva, the magnets of the large particle accelerator LHC are cooled to about 1.9 kelvin. That is colder than empty space, which has a temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. This leftover heat comes from the time shortly after the Big Bang. The coldest natural places in space are gas clouds such as the Boomerang Nebula, at about 1 kelvin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero.
A measure of how strongly the smallest particles move.
A substance that conducts electricity without loss when very cold.
The science of heat and energy.

gewusst: In Fahrenheit, absolute zero is about minus 460 degrees.
Inside the particle accelerator at CERN it is colder than in empty space.
Even at absolute zero the particles would still jiggle very slightly because of quantum physics.

teile.einleitung: The Basel Carnival, or Fasnacht, is the biggest carnival in Switzerland and lasts exactly 72 hours. It begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday at 4 o’clock in the morning with the Morgestraich, when all the lights in the city centre go out. The people of Basel lovingly call it “die drey scheenschte Dääg”, the three most beautiful days.
wichtigste: The Basel Carnival begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday.
It starts with the Morgestraich at 4 o’clock in the morning.
It lasts three days and ends at 4 o’clock on Thursday morning.
Typical features are piccolos, drums, masks and large lanterns.
The carnival participants are organised in groups called cliques.
Since 2017 it has been part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.
Confetti is called “Räppli” in Basel.

abschnitte.text: On the Monday at **4 o’clock** sharp, all the street lamps in Basel’s city centre are switched off. At the command “Morgestraich, vorwärts, marsch!” (forward, march!) the cliques set off. They carry glowing **lanterns** with pictures and verses that often make fun of the year’s events. Thousands of spectators stand in the dark at the roadside.

The typical music of the Basel Carnival is played on **piccolos** and **drums**. The marches have names such as “Arabi” or “Morgestraich”. Many children learn the piccolo or drums early and practise all year round. Then there are the loud **Guggenmusik** bands with brass instruments, which give their big concert on Tuesday evening.

The carnival participants wear large masks, which in Basel are called **Larven**. A well-known character is the **Waggis**, a farmer from Alsace with a big nose and a blue smock. It is important to stay unrecognised; this is called “intrigieren”. The colourful **Blaggedde**, a badge to pin on, is also part of it and supports the carnival financially.

On Monday and Wednesday afternoons the big parade, the **Cortège**, moves through the city. The floats hand out oranges, sweets and flowers, but also throw Räppli. In the evening, **Schnitzelbänke** go round restaurants and cellars. They sing short, witty verses about politics and the events of the year.

Carnival has a long history in Basel going back to the Middle Ages. Unlike most Catholic carnivals, it only takes place after Ash Wednesday, because Basel became Protestant at the Reformation. Each year about 18,000 active participants take part. In 2017 **UNESCO** added the Basel Carnival to the list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The start of the Basel Carnival on Monday at 4 o’clock in the morning.
A group that performs together at the carnival.
Basel word for a carnival mask.
Basel word for confetti.
A group that performs mocking verses about current events.

gewusst: If you get showered with Räppli at the carnival, you often find them in your pockets and shoes weeks later.
During the Morgestraich even taking photos with a flash is frowned upon, so that the lanterns can have their effect.
